speechtext: Mr. A. W. NEILL (Comox-Alberni) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 122 respecting Immigration.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Explain.

This is a mild and modest bill. It is non-contentious and I think it should receive the support of every hon. member. It provides that immigrants coming to Canada shall first apply for permission to do so; they shall write from the country of their origin asking for that permission and stating their qualifications, and they can be accepted or rejected at the discretion of the Government. There is a provision in this exempting people of British birth. Primarily it is intended to do away with the injustice, of which we have had evidence even so recently as during the present session, where immigrants coming to Canada from a distance are rejected at the point of arrival. Sometimes families are broken up by reason of one of their members being found undesirable and being deported. This causes great hardship and expense to immigrants, and such an undesirable condition would be obviated by the bill which I now introduce, because intending immigrants would have to state their nationality, their ages, their resources, and the facts regarding their health. The bill requires that these facts shall be stated in a letter of application, and the immigrants can be accepted or rejected as the government sees fit. That is the primary object; but incidentally- quite incidentally-I think it would solve the problem in connection with oriental immigration in the West. There is no mention of Orientals, or Japanese, or exclusion, but the exclusion of these people is secured by the simple method I have stated. I shall not detain the House on the subject at this stage; it can be discussed on the second reading. I would, however, strongly commend the matter to the serious attention of the House and of the Government. I believe that the proposed bill provides a simple and unassailable form of dealing with the Asiatic and oriental problem in the West.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

I beg to call the attention of the Government to the following despatch, dated from London, May 26:
Many British Artisans preparing to make their Homes in Canada.
Relaxation of Dominion's Immigration Regulations Results in Increase of Men Coming Who are Out of Johs in Britain
London, May 26,-(Montreal Gazette Cable) -A considerable increase in the movement of British artisans to Canada is expected as a result of the relaxation of the Dominion's Immigration regulations. The orders-in-council having arrived from Canada, the Dominion Immigration Offices here issued copies of the modified regulations to the steamship agencies to-day. They show that cabled reports to the British press were incorrect and that the ihanges are infinitely more far-reaching than reported. The removal of all occupational restrictions for British subjects is regarded here as the most important change of all. In the past, the immigration of the artisan class was allowed only where such labour was unobtainable in Canada. Now any workman may enter if he has enough funds to sustain himself until he secures employment. With industrial conditions what they are in Great Britain, it is thought

that many will avail themselves of the opportunity of seeking to better their condition by going to Canada.
In view of the fact that we have such a large volume of unemployment in Canada, may I ask if there is any protection for the artisans in this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior) :
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is true that the money qualification of $250 formerly exacted has been removed, but notwithstanding that fact care is being exercised by the officials of the Immigration Department to impress upon intending immigrants to Canada who are looking for immediate employment that no work in the artisan classes is available, but that there is abundant room for agricultural labourers, household' workers, and others who are able to purchase land or have sufficient means to support themselves in Canada.
The fact is, then, that the protection hitherto afforded the artisans of this country is removed; am I right in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
understand what particular protection my hon. friend refers to. The regulation requiring an immigrant to possess $250 no longer obtains, but full information is given intending immigrants who expect to secure immediate employment on arrival that they are in a sense in the restricted classes. If, however, they have sufficient means to maintain themselves, there is no bar to their coming in.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speakeroldname: Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: RIGHTS ENJOYED BY CANADIANS IN JAPAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to make
a correction in an answer to a question by the hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie) with regard to the enjoyment of certain rights by Canadians in Japan, which question and answer will be found in Han- [DOT] sard of May 5th at pages 1513 and 1514.
The answer relates to the right of Canadian labourers to pursue their callings in Japan. In the last paragraph of answer No. 2 it is stated .that:
Foreign labourers may not pursue their callings in Japan outside the limits of the former foreign settlements or the "mixed residence" areas without the express permission of the administrative authorities.

Immigration
I am informed by Mr. Ohta, the Japanese Consul General in Ottawa, that this answer is bound to lead to a misconception. The Japanese Imperial Ordinance No. 352, dated the 28th July, 1899, provides that all aliens, regardless of the fact that some of them are not entitled by treaty or customary practice to freedom of residence in Japan, may reside, move or pursue their callings in any place outside the former foreign settlements or the "mixed residence" areas.
The Japanese Government, mainly in order to ameliorate the restrictions that had been put upon Chinese labourers, promulgated the above Ordinance with a proviso that alien labourers coming from countries having no commercial treaty with Japan or not entitled by customary practice to do so, may not pursue their callings outside the limits of the former foreign settlements or the "mixed residence" areas without the permission of the administrative authorities. It is needless to say, therefore, so Mr. Ohta informs me, that Canadian citizens, irrespective of their calling -labourer or non-labourer-stand outside the scope of this ordinance and are fully entitled to engage in business, etc., in any place within Japanese territory in common with the nationals of the most favoured nation.	[DOT]
In connection with the matter of land holding by aliens in Japan I am further informed by Mr. Ohta, who in these matters is advised and instructed by the Minister for Foreign Affairs at Tokio, that there is provided in the Japanese Civil Code a title of lease of movable and immovable property (besides the superficies and emphyteusis mentioned in No. 2 of the same answer) which all aliens alike with Japanese subjects can obtain for a period of not longer than twenty years; and further that the lease and emphyteusis (the term of the latter is from twenty to fifty years) can be renewed and the superficies can be created for any number of years by contract, tending practically to obliterate the difference from the ownership of land.
Consequently it is maintained by the Japanese Government that foreign residents in Japan are not subject to the least inconvenience in the leasing and holding of land, nor do they complain of the restrictions which still exist with respect to land ownership by an individual alien and which the Japanese Go vernment hopes soon to remove.
I felt, Mr. Speaker, that in view of the answer which was given on the 5th instant I should at once direct the attention of the House to this correction as soon as it was brought to my notice.

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Argenteuil, Minister of the Interior) :
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. 
Speaker, I do not intend to take up very much of the time of the House this afternoon in discussing the budget; I wish shortly to direct the attention of hon. members, if I can, to the situation prevailing in Canada with which the Government has to contend at the moment. Let me first, however, congratulate my friend and colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) on the long and valuable service which he has been able to render to the people of Canada, both as Minister of Finance, and, for a short time, as critic of the measures offered by the government in office. His career might well, I think, be the envy of all parliamentarians. Perhaps not many will live to sit in Parliament during sixteen sessions, much less to deliver sixteen budget speeches. Perhaps none of us will have the opportunity of being identified so long with the public life of Canada or of attaining the experience that my hon. friend must bring to matters of national finance.
One cannot very well discuss present conditions in Canada without looking backward. But in dealing with this matter I wish to approach it in no critical mood; I simply wish to trace some of the principal events which have occurred in the political life of Canada since the introduction of what was known in our young days as the National Policy. The introduction of that policy had the effect of concentrating industry in the larger centres of eastern Canada; it had a tendency to bring about the establishment in urban centres-in Toronto, Montreal, Brantford, and a few centres of that character-the manufacturing industry which had formerly been centred in the smaller towns and villages of Ontario and of eastern Canada generally. I remember very well that in 1890 I was engaged in agriculture in the old province of Ontario. It has been said that during the past year we have been passing through the most critical period, so far as agriculture is concerned, that Canada has seen in its history. My recollection is that during the years from 1892 until at least 1895, we had a much more serious condition of affairs, so far as agricultural pursuits were concerned, than has prevailed even in recent times. Not only that, similar conditions prevailed in our industrial life. I lived in the county of Simcoe in those days, and I will remember meeting a mechanic who had travelled all the way from St. John, New Brunswick, to that part of Ontario without securing employment. The conditions were said to be so severe that

The Budget-Mr. C. Stewart
we might never recover from them, and it was affirmed that the policy that had been pursued by the government was not in the best interests of Canada; that a protectionist policy had brought about those conditions. Mr. Speaker, although I have been an ardent Liberal all my life, I do not think I would be (prepared to blame the fiscal policy of the government of the day for all the difficulties experienced at that time. But that it had something to do with them, I think we will all agree. In 1896, you will remember, Sir Wilfrid Laurier came into power and the Liberal party took office. Although some changes in the matter of fiscal policy did take place-changes, for instance, affecting the exportation of our cattle-they were criticized by hon. gentlemen then in opposition from much the same point of view that the present fiscal policy has been criticized: on the ground that the changes were not sufficient to bring about the desired result. I do not intend to enter into the matter in detail, but it has been frequently stated that the period from 1896 to 1911 was one of the most prosperous periods that Canada has enjoyed since Confederation, nor am I going to claim that that was wholly due to the policy of the government of the day. Anyone who studies the matter closely will agree that there are cycles in the history of every country in which prosperity seems to reach the highest pinnacle and is then succeeded by a period of depression. Notwithstanding the efforts that may be put forth by governments, we do have periods of extreme deflation. At best, all the government is able to do is by legislation, in as large a sense as possible, to afford relief, in those places where it seems to be necessary from the effects that may result upon trade or upon the business of the country.
In 1911 a change of government took place. I think every hon. member who comes from western Canada will agree that at least from our viewpoint a serious mistake was made when reciprocity was rejected by the people of Canada. Be that as it may, that was the decision of the people. Those who have been in public life for any considerable length of time know that changes take place, men step in and out by the will of the people; so that no one need quarrel with their decision. But as I remember conditions in 1914 just prior to the outbreak of the war, we had in western Canada a serious situation. There was a great deal of unemployment-and I think that was true also of eastern Canada. Then the war broke out and the whole force of Canada was thrown into the war effort; political questions were, for the moment, lost sight of, and we joined hand in hand in the determination to win. Naturally this has imposed a tremendous obligation upon Canada. During all these years there have been growing up, mainly in the eastern part of Canada, but gradually extending westward, strong manufacturing organizations. And alongside of that development the plains of western Canada have been settled by farmers, little towns have grown up, and small industries have been established; but in the main the business of the people of western Canada, and indeed of the people of all Canada, is that of agriculture.
During this period some reduction in the tariff took place-I am speaking now of the period from 1911 forward-but not any very serious changes. There was a slight reduction in the tariff on farm implements, more particularly those most used on the farms. I see my hon. friends smiling. I want to be absolutely fair about this thing, so that we shall arrive at a proper understanding. There was, I say, a slight reduction in the tariff on farm implements, and in order to help the Greater Production campaign put on by the late government, tractors were put upon the free list. This, no doubt, had some effect in assisting agriculture, since any reducton in the tariff upon the implements of production, no matter of what kind, is bound to afford some relief. On the other hand, during the war period this country assumed tremendous obligations. Our public debt increased from $336,000,000 until in 1921 it stood at $2,427,296,789. This tremendous obligation was incurred through the prosecution of the war, and this public debt is an overhead charge that must be taken into account in considering tariff changes. Not only that; just before the close of the war every endeavour of the Canadian people in all lines and in every artery was directed towards the production of war material, and of war material alone, and in consequence, at the end of the war, we found our stocks for home consumption very much depleted. I well remember discussing these matters with the premiers of the western provinces on the day the armistice was signed, and the one thing we had in mind then was the securing of employment, the re-establishing of the men who would be returning from overseas, which we anticipated would be somewhat early. We did not anticipate that for two or three years there would

The Budget-Mr. C. Stewart
be a period of inflation in manufacturing and business generally. The drop that we expected to occur after the signing of the armistice when we had to absorb all these men, did not come. On the contrary, the manufacturers of this country found their plants working at full speed in order to make up for the depletion that had taken place in stocks for ordinary home consumption during the war. We. passed through two or three years of this period, and it was perhaps our period of greatest prosperity, for two years at least. Speaking of western Canada more particularly, m 1920 the farmer who had a crop never had a bigger one, and never got a better price for it. Unfortunately for western Canada, in many areas there was no crop at all and had not been for a number of years. A great portion of our difficulty arises from the fact that our farming industry has been patchy for the last three or four years.
Then what happened? In 1921, the increased activity in manufacturing that had followed the signing of the armistice came to a sudden stop; business was at a standstill, and manufacturers and merchants found their warehouses and shops filled with goods, with no one to buy them. The farmers who reaped a crop in 1921 had great difficulty in disposing of it, they found that the crop, which had been raised at an enormous cost had dropped back to pre-war prices. So, almost overnight, foliowing the period of inflation, manufacturers, merchants and farmers, in fact the whole people of Canada, found themselves in an embarrassing situation. The manufacturers were forced to stop producing, and the farmers were unable to meet their obligations. These difficulties continued for a year or two. One of the reasons for these difficulties, so far as agriculture is concerned, is that we were not favoured with good crops. If I may cite the experience on my own farm, I made more money in the years prior to the war than I did during the war period. That was largely because, except in one or two years of the war period, we were not favoured with weather conditions that enabled us to reap a full crop. The conditions I have described applied from one end of Canada to the other, and to-day we find ourselves taking stock. The agriculturists complain that conditions are such as have never before prevailed m Canada. I take issue with that. I say that we did in 1892 have similar conditions, and in my opinion they were even worse, 
but we recovered, and we had similar conditions in the industrial world from 1892 to 1894, but we also recovered from that.
I agree with one thing that my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) said, that we need' a larger spirit of optimism in connection with these matters than perhaps we admit upon all occasions. In addition to the great public debt with which the people of Canada find themselves saddled to-day, another obligation has fallen upon our shoulders. The great privately-owned railway system that in the days of our prosperity we fondly hoped we should require in its entirety, has practically all become the property of the government. Railways were built in all parts of Canada, and there was duplication to some extent, and to-day we find ourselves with these roads on our hands. I am not finding fault particularly with the position in which we find ourselves with respect to the national railways, but I say that there can be no question that the railway problem adds to the responsibilities of government and to the difficulties in carrying on public affairs, inasmuch as these utilities are not self-sustaining but year after year are faced with a deficit upon operation, in addition to their fixed charges. While the policy has been pursued of relegating to the future the charges that accrue from year to year upon our railways, I question if the people of Canada can continue that policy very much longer. I think many of us who are interested in the public operation of these utilities will agree that there must be a time when the fixed charges upon them must cease; that we cannot keep on piling up deficits in operation and adding fixed charges to the capitalization of these corporations. Very shortly, if not indeed at once the revenues of Canada will have to be drawn upon to take care of deficits in operation as well as the fixed charges, or else the overcapitalization upon the railways will be such that it will be utterly impossible at any time, under any circumstances, for these railways to meet their obligations. The $466,938,359 of ordinary expenditure, shown by the Minister of Finance, for this year would look like a fairly respectable burden for a population of less than nine millions of people to meet. In addition there is an overhead upon our railways of some seventy-two million odd dollars, accounted for by interest charges and expected deficits in operation.
Very little criticism, except of a captious character so far as I can learn, has been

The Budget-Mr. C. Stewart
offered of the budget presented last week. In some quarters the contention has been made that there is no real tariff reduction. Indeed, I think, that is the criticism offered by the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton)-that the tariff reduction made is not worth while, is not effective, and that it is more than wiped out by increased taxation. The basis of the criticism offered by the hon. gentleman rests upon the policy adopted by the Liberal Convention in this city in 1919, upon which occasion it was definitely set out that the aim of the Liberals of Canada, practically, was that there should be no duty upon the implements of production. I have not the resolution then adopted at present before me, but at all events that is what it meant. The accusation is made that the Liberal party won the last election upon the terms of that resolution. On the other hand the Minister of Finance cited a resolution moved by him at the last session of parliament which, he claimed, set out the situation as it existed at that time. We must admit that a situation has arisen, not only in Canada but in the United States as well, that we cannot help but take note of it. In 1919 we had a reasonable assurance that the reciprocity agreement negotiated in 1911 might be accepted by the United States in part if not in full, but to-day that hope has disappeared; the Fordney Bill introduced at Washington places upon imports of natural products from Canada into the United States tariff restrictions that were unheard of in the past. We have in Canada to-day a difficult situation as regards the agricultural and manufacturing industries; and I believe this is the time when the government should move slowly and carefully in the direction of removing duties on any articles instead of advancing with any rapidity. My hon. friend from Strathcona (Mr. Warner), speaking the other night said that it would be a very difficult thing for the Minister of Interior to go back and secure a seat in the province of Alberta. Perhaps it would; I did not secure a seat in that province at the last election. When the opportunity comes I shall endeavour to secure one; but until that time does come I will have to abide the consequences; I have always been willing to accept the results of any political warfare. I have little or no disagreement with my hon. friend from Strathcona, or any of my hon. friends sitting opposite. That, I think, is not the spirit in which we can secure what is necessary to revive agricultural and business interests in Canada. Rather we should all get together in this connection if that be at all possible. When it came to the question of selecting articles upon which tariff reductions should be made I think the Minister of Finance exercised due care in trying, so far as it was humanly possible, to avoid the disturbance of business and agricultural interests. That policy undoubtedly does not meet with the approval of many of my hon. friends. Perhaps it does not go as far as even I should be willing to go in this matter, but I am convinced of this fact: That it would be unwise to be too drastic at this time when there is hope-and in my opinion a very great hope-for the revival of the agricultural industry; when perhaps there is the prospect of a better system of marketing our wheat; and when more attention is being paid to the securing of markets abroad, which, I think, is one of the important things this government must undertake and pursue to the fullest possible extent. When these things are accomplished, as they must be accomplished -because it is an utter impossibility that we can thrive agriculturally in Western Canada, or indeed that business can be carried on successfully in Eastern Canada with the high freight rates prevailing to-day; and, of course, we have the assertion of the railway companies that they cannot operate with insufficient freight rates-then we can look with hope to the future.
I am not going to discuss the freight rate question at any length because it is at present before a special committee and a report will shortly be forthcoming from that committee. But let me say that this is, in my opinion, one of the very great factors in connection with the revival of our trade in Canada. It is of great importance that we should have a reduction in freight rates and better marketing facilities; these will help us in a much larger degree than any attempt at the moment to deal drastically with the tariff. The government is being criticized very severely because of the tariff reductions it has already made. For the life of me I cannot understand why that should be so, except that people get into the habit of living under a protection, and we may be sure that they will raise a commotion when you touch them at any quarter. On the other hand, we cannot ignore the fact that to-day we are largely shut out from the United States

The Budget-Mr. C. Stewart
markets by the tariff wall erected by the Fordney tariff. But it must be borne in mind that we have not been slow in notifying the United States government that, as soon as they are ready to do business with us in connection with tariff reductions or interchange of trade, this Government is ready to deal with them. Therefore, all that I desire to say this afternoon is that, having in mind the condition in which we find agriculture and other business to-day, and the commercial relationships that exist throughout Canada, it seems to me that this Government was well advised to move cautiously with respect to tariff reductions.
We have been criticised with respect to the new taxation. I have tried briefly to show you the obligations of the people of Canada and to bring to your attention the fact that we cannot continue to postpone payment from the revenues of Canada of the losses accruing annually on the railways of the country, and, that sooner or later, we must take care that they shall grow no larger, if we are to make a success of this enterprise. Having these things in mind, we must, of necessity, have a much greater revenue than that obtained in the past, and, in order to secure that revenue, the policy of the Government has been, as far as possible, to avoid placing upon any industry or business an undue burden of taxation. I think it is a safe axiom with respect to taxation, that you must tax the people who can best afford to pay, and tax industry where it can best afford to be taxed. I think there is a comparative unanimity of feeling with respect to the sales tax, which, perhaps, we have made a little more severe; and it may be contended in some measure by our friends in the Opposition that we should have taxed luxuries to a far greater extent than we have. That may very well be a matter for consideration. One of my hon. friends, in discussing this matter the Dther day, mentioned the fact that the income tax was not sufficiently severe in so far as large incomes were concerned. It is not as severe, Mr. Speaker, as the income tax of Great Britain, one will admit, but that it is a fairly stiff tax on incomes of large dimensions, no one will deny. The question whether the individual who is in receipt of a smaller income should not be given some consideration is a matter, perhaps, which might very well be considered at some future time. It is an extremely easy matter to 
4	p.m. suggest the placing of taxatior upon luxuries, and I agree wit! the suggestion that it is an easy mattei to suggest that the taxation should be heavier on the larger incomes. There may be something to be said about that. On the whole, the income tax and taxation of that character seem to be fairly well adjusted. I am not saying there should not be a readjustment. There will, of necessity, require to be a readjustment. The one object we have had in view in placing taxes upon business has been to avoid taxing the basic industries. If we have not succeeded in that-[DOT] and undoubtedly many hon. members will disagree with us on that point-on the whole, I think it has met with a very favourable reception by the people of Canada, and I trust it will meet out our expectations, and that we will not be adding to the public debt of Canada, what, in my opinion at all events, rightfully should have been charged to the revenue account annually. I feel that the effort of the hon. Minister of Finance will not perhaps satisfy my hon. friends of the official Opposition in that it goes too far, and, my hon. friends of the Progressive element in that it does not go far enough; but the Government, having in mind all the conditions that prevailed in Canada, felt that this effort in reduction of the tariff, as well as in the raising of revenue, would meet with fairly generous approval throughout the whole of Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words this afternoon will be words of congratulation and appreciation of the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), who has been permitted to introduce his sixteenth budget in a Canadian parliament. Those of us from Western Canada have a very warm spot in our hearts for the hon. Minister of Finance. We remember that in 1911, through his efforts, an arrangement was entered into with the United States for reciprocal trade in natural products. We remember also that, in endeavouring to give effect to that arrangement, he and his party went down to defeat, but not through any fault of the electors of the province from which I come, because we returned to this parliament ninety per cent of our representatives as supporters of reciprocity with the United States. I also wish to congratulate the hon. minister on his courage in placing before this House and the country the true financial position of Canada. It is not a nice thing to review, and I am sure the minister himself must have felt the task a

The Budget-Mr. J. F. Johnston
very heavy one, having regard to the budgets that he had been privileged to present to this House in years gone by. In those days our revenues were buoyant, and he was able to tell the country that we had a surplus, instead of a deficit. But on this occasion he told the House that the income of Canada for the last year was fifty-three millions some 'hundred thousand dollars odd less than the year previous. He also informed us that the estimated revenue for the incoming year was $134,000,000 less than his estimated expenditure-not a very nice picture to present to any body of people. Nevertheless, it is a fact, and he stated it to the House. He also informed the House that, during the last year, we added eighty-six and a half millions to the national debt of the country-something for my horn, friends to the right of me to contemplate. We were told that during the period that has elapsed since the cessation of hostilities Great Britain has paid off some five hundred million pounds of her war debt while we continued to add to ours. My hon. friends to the right are always ready to take the credit for everything that was done during the war; I hope they are just as ready to shoulder the responsibility for this condition of affairs. The fact remains, nevertheless, that by reason of our participation in the war there has been added to the national debt over $2,000,000,000, while during the last decade our population has increased very slightly. The result is that the citizens of Canada have shouldered a very heavy obligation in the way of increased taxation. While I do not like being retrospective, I cannot refrain from saying that in my opinion the heavy taxes imposed upon the people at the present time could, to some degree at least, have been avoided had former governments, during the war particularly, taxed wealth where they had a chance to do so. I have no criticism for the immediate predecessor (Sir Henry Drayton) of the Minister of Finance. As a matter of fact, I think he did what he could. But the Minister of Finance who held office during the war lost a real chance, in my opinion, to tax war wealth during that period. The profiteers have escaped and taken to cover, and we are now faced with the responsibility of raising huge sums, when our people are little able to bear heavy taxation, and at a time when we have great unemployment in the country. During the election campaign we Progressives contended that this was a time when the most stringent economy should be practised in Canada, and that contention has been amply borne out by the statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) as presented to Parliament a few days ago.
I come now to a very brief review of the reductions in the tariff and the increase in the sales tax. I wish to say to the Minister of Finance and the Government that the reductions in the customs tariff are good in so far as they go; but the great trouble is that they do not go far enough. While I am sure we all appreciated the splendid effort of the minister in presenting his budget, I could not help thinking, while he was repeating the reductions, nearly all of which were 21 per cent, that one might very well suppose himself out in the countryside at an auction sale where the auctioneer was experiencing great difficulty in getting the bidders to go above a very low minimum, because it was 21 per cent, and 21 per cent, and again 21 per cent, all the way through. I could have hoped, for the sake of variety at least, that the minister had departed somewhat from this even tenor and taken an upward trend. I am sorry that these reductions are not greater, because I believe that if they were we should have a materially increased production in the country. In the matter of tariffs, it strikes me that we Canadians are very much in the position of a man stuck in the mire trying to pull himself out by his shoestrings; he might work very assiduously, but the only result would be that he would bury himself further, and finally be engulfed. If we are to increase production and put this country in that position which is rightly hers, we shall not do so by conceding 21 per cent reductions on the necessities of life and on the implements of production that are needed by those people who, in my opinion, are the real wealth producers of Canada.
Now, as regards the increase in the sales tax, I can only describe this as bad; I cannot view it from any other standpoint. And in imposing this increase of fifty per cent in this tax the minister, in effect, takes away with one hand what he gives with the other. It is true that the revenue derived from the imposition of this increase in the sales tax will, or at least should, all find its way into the public treasury, while under the customs duties only about one dollar in three or four finds its way there. Having regard to that fact I favour the sales tax as against the customs tariff. But this tax is imposed at a time when our people are least able to bear it; it takes from the people not in proportion to their
2222	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. J. F. Johnston
ability to pay but in proportion to their purchase of goods. It takes from the poor man with a family of between five and ten children and a salary of $1,000, equally as it takes from the man with the income of $50,000 or from the millionaire. No one can gainsay that. Under the imposition of the new taxes, we have not attempted, in this budget, to tax wealth, or to exact from it any heavier taxes. Why, then, should we at this time impose this fifty per cent increase upon the workers of the land? Let us view this matter in relation to immigration into, and emigration from, this country. There is no such tax levied in the United States; there is no general sales tax. If such a tax had been imposed in that country last year the government would have received $850,000.000. So that there is some inducement for our labouring classes, under the circumstances, to go to the United States. It is obvious that we are placing our people in a much worse position than the labourers of the United States are in. I sincerely hope that the Government do not view the sales tax as a permanent fixture in our scheme of taxation.
In connection with the income tax assessment, we give some regard, in the matter of exemptions, to the man with the small salary. Under that act we grant that it takes $2,000 for a married man to live, and we accordingly exempt him up to that amount. We also give him $200 exemption on every dependent child. Under the sales tax, however, there is absolutely no exemption. In the United States, on the other hand, they assum.. that it takes $2,500 for a man and wife to live, and they give an exemption for dependent children up to $400. We give no exemption to any classes under the sales tax, so that the man with a salary of $500 or $1,000 is in just the same position, in this regard, as the man with the income of $50,000.
So far my remarks might be termed critical; but I have always endeavoured, when I have found it necessary to criticise or tear down anything, to offer something in its place. I shall therefore try to give what seems to me to be the solution of our problems. I think these might very well be classified under three heads: First, immigration; second, increased production; and third, wider and better markets.
Now, in regard to immigration, what is the situation? We find that during the last decade we have lost over 1,250,000 of our people. We have in Canada to-day a

population of 8,725,000. Had we held the immigrants that came to our shores during the past decade we should have had, with the natural increase in population, 11,000,000 people in the country to-day. It seems to me that we might be very well employed, when considering immigration matters, in giving some thought to this fact, and in trying to find out why we are losing our people. Is it good business for Canada to continue spending money in bringing people into this country by the front door while the51' are going oue by way of the back door? And yet that is what has been happening. No one will deny, Mr. Speaker, that we have a country capable of sustaining many times our present population. All are agreed on that. And what w;e should attempt to solve is the ques+ion why we cannot hold the people that we do get. I have my own opinion about this, and it is briefly stated. Before .we can hope to hold our population we must of necessity change the economic conditions under which these people have to labour. I have stated in this House before that you never find people running away from a good thing; and they are not going to leave Canada if Canada gives them an opportunity to make good. I could recite many unsatisfactory conditions as they exist, but I am not here to decry the country that we all love so well, nor to paint conditions as they exist to-day in western Canada in a blacker hue than has already been done. None of us want to do that. But it seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that if western Canada is to be given any redress, plain words must be spoken in this Parliament. I submit, then, that if we are to solve our immigration problem we must remove the obstacles that prevent our people undertaking the development of our natural resources, or that hinder those already engaged in that development.
In regard to increased production, according to a recent survey, we have ill western Canada within fifteen miles of existing lines of railway some 25,000,000 or 30,000,000 acres of arable land. Last year we produced about 300,000,000 bushels of wheat. Our average yield per acre is 34 bushels. If we bring this 25,000,000 acres of vacant land under cultivation we would have a return of 350,000,000 bushels of wheat, or 16 per cent more than our total yield last year. Now, in solving our immigration problem we would, in a large degree, solve our railway problem, for the increase in our population would lead to
222J

The Budget-Mr. J. F. Johnston
the increase in our wheat production, which in turn would help our railways. Railways exist on freight and passenger traffic- mainly the former. If we can give our railways 16 per cent more wheat to haul, and the like amount of incoming freight, we will have gone a long way toward solving that problem. And there is no disputing the fact that it is an urgent problem, because we all know that our National Railways were operated at a deficit of $72,000,000 this year, a slight improvement over the preceding year when the deficit was $2,500,000 more. These matters are fundamental and should have the earnest consideration of the Government.
As to wider markets, I would revert to the attempt made by my hon. friend, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) in 1911, and I wish to congratulate and to thank him for making another endeavour a few months ago to effect a better trade arrangement with the United States. My right hon. friend who leads the official Opposition (Mr. Meighen) and those associated with him, during their term of office put through certain trade agreements with France and the British West Indies. It may surprise my right hon. friend to know that during the late campaign I gave to him and his party every credit for widening Canada's markets to that extent. But, if it was good business for Canada to enter into trade agreements with France and the British West Indies, I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it would be much better business for us to make every endeavour to arrange a trade agreement with the United States. Last year our exports to the United States amounted to $542,322,000, with imports to the value of $856,176,000; to France $27,000,000 and $19,000,000 respectively; to the British West Indies $16,000,000 and $24,000,000 respectively. A comparison of these figures will show that we did more business with the United States in two weeks than we did with the British West Indies in the whole fifty-two weeks; and that we did more business with the United States in three weeks than we did with France during the whole year. So, I repeat, if it is good business to effect trade agreements with France and the British West Indies, it follows that it is much better business to enter into a trade agreement with the United States. But, although my hon. friends to the right negotiated those trade agreements with France and the British West Indies, yet they are opposed to closer trade relations with the
United States. Their attitude is very hard to understand. In view of the fact that wider markets are so essential to the development of our country.
In connection with the question of better markets, I wish to mention a matter that has been engaging the attention of one of our standing committees for some weeks, and will very shortly be brought before this House in a definite way. For that reason I propose only to mention it; I refer to the Wheat Board. Despite anything that has been said, I feel that the farmers of western Canada are entitled to some kind of selling agency to handle their wheat crop. And I wish to dispel the erroneous idea that has gotten into the minds of the people of eastern Canada that as a result of the formation of such a board flour and wheat products will cost more to our Canadian consumers than would otherwise be the case. That is an absolutely wrong impression, Mr. Speaker. In the marketing of our wheat I have always felt that we as producers have been our worst enemies November 1 is settlement day in. western Canada; when the banks, the implement manufacturing firms, and so on, are looking to the farmer to settle his accounts. The result is that the wheat is rushed onto the market and sold whether or not there is a real demand for it. Last year the United States, knowing the conditions in Britain and Europe, rushed their exportable surplus onto the market early, with the result that when the Canadian western wheat became available, the demand for wheat on the other side had been, for the time being, supplied. Our wheat was forced on the market; the producers being driven to sell by their creditors, with the result that the market was glutted and great depression in prices ensued. That is all that the western producer is asking for-an agency to step in there, take control of that wheat, supply the market when there is a demand and hold the wheat off the market when there is no demand. I believe it will result in benefit to the producer as well as to every class of people in this country if the [producer is enabled to get what his commodity will bring on the open market. That is all we are asking. The western wheat producer is not asking for protection or for special privilege.
I now come, Mr. Speaker, to a brief consideration of the amendment moved by the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton). The hon. member and those associated with him are condemning

The Budget-Mr. J. F. Johnston
the Government for not doing something which he and those associated with him would not themselves do. They are condemning the Government through this amendment for not doing what he and all the supporters of his party said during the last campaign would bring blue ruin to Canada if it were put into effect. He is condemning the Government for committing a great sin against the political morality of this country; yet he and those behind this motion are not, so far as I can see, doing anything else than carrying out a little political manoeuvering for party advantage. Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I want to make my position clear. I criticise the Government from a wholly different angle-because they have not given effect to their platform as it has been quoted in the amendment before the House. Now, I am going to read that part of the amendment, Mr. Speaker, because it appeals to me. If one goes to a restaurant and is presented with a good menu, he is apt to go back there again; and this, to me, is a very good menu. I am going to read this declaration of policy in order that it may be incorporated in the few remarks which I am making, and also to bring it again to the attention of the Government. It says:
That to these ends, wheat, wheat flour and all products of wheat; the principal articles of food; farm implements and machinery; farm tractors; mining, flour and saw mill machinery and repair parts thereof; rough and partly dressed lumber; gasoline, illuminating, lubricating and fuel oils; nets, net twines, and fishermen's equipments ; cements, and fertilizers, should be free from customs duties, as well as the raw material entering into same.
That the British preference be increased to 50 per cent of the general tariff.
And the Liberal Party hereby pledges itself to implement by legislation the provisions of this resolution when returned to power.
That is a good bill of fare, Mr, Speaker. I subscribe to every word of it, and I criticise the Government, not that I would have expected them to go the whole road this session, but that they have not gone further than they have. I had looked with every confidence to the Government to bring down a progressive policy at this time. To say that I am disappointed is putting it mildly, because I believe that if we as a people are ever going to get out of the woods, so to speak, we shall have to right-about-face on this policy of ours. We have been endeavouring for over forty years to make something of this country under a protective policy; we see where we have landed, and I am sorry that the Government have not given us a lead in

the other direction. I can only hope that before another session the Government will have considered the matter and will come to Parliament with a much different statement from that with which we have been greeted this year.
I want to say, Mr. Speaker, in conclusion-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the annual national accounting was looked forward to with greater interest than usual this year, because most people in Canada knew that the times were abnormal and that all was not well with the country, but I think a good many did r.ot realize to the full the seriousness of the situation. I think even some members of the House even now, including the hon. exMinister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) do not fully realize the gravity of present conditions.
Let us consider for a moment just what are the present conditions. To begin with, the net debt of Canada is $2,428,000,000, and that does not include the railway bond guarantees of $300,000,000 odd. If these were included, the net debt would be two and three-quarter billions, and the gross debt over three billions of dollars. We have the revenues decreasing, and the national debt increasing at the rate of about $90,000,000 a year. These figures are so large that the ordinary person cannot comprehend them; I know I cannot. Perhaps we can understand the situation a little better by looking at it from another point of view. The interest alone (last year was $140,000,000, or an amount equal to the total expenditure on all accounts-consolidated fund, capital account, and all other accounts-in the years immediately preceding the war. If we add to the interest, the thirty-six or thirty-seven million dollars for soldiers' pensions, and other commitments incurred on account of the soldiers' civil re-establishment, we have nearly $200,000,000, or an amount twice as large as the expenditure on consolidated fund in the years immediately preceding the war. These obligations have to be met before we have a dollar for civil government, for transportation, for public works, and for the thousand and one other things necessary to carry on the public business of the country. That is the situation.
How are we to raise the enormous sums that must be provided? This year the estimated expenditure as already submitted to Parliament amounts, in round figures, to $469,000,000, with the Supplementary Estimates still to come, and which will probably bring the figure up to $500,000,000, after all
the economies that have been practicable have been made. Where is the money to come from? Just from two sources-further taxation and from borrowing, or from both. We are running into debt at the rate of eighty or ninety million dollars per year. Can that go on indefinitely? Everybody knows it cannot. A nation can run into bankruptcy just the same as an individual. We also owe in the United States, according to an article I read in the Financial Post a short time ago, on federal, provincial, municipal, and industrial account, something like seven or eight hundred million dollars, and that is expected to amount to one 'billion dollars in the near future.
Can greater economies be effected? Economy can be carried too far. There is a policy that scattereth yet increaseth, and there is a policy that withholdet'h but tend-eth to poverty. Transportation by land and water must be provided for; the public works of the country must be provided for; for if these things are starved, the industrial life of the nation is injured or destroyed and the sources of revenue are dried up. Therefore, economy can be carried too far. Can taxation be carried too far? Yes, because if you tax an individual or a company to the point of taking all the profits, and leave the individual or the company to take all1 the risks and all the losses, you drive capital out of business. Individuals or companies will not take all the risk unless they have a reasonable expectation of making a fair profit. If the government steps in and by taxation takes all the profits, it dries up the sources of revenue, and the country is injured greatly.
Can borrowing go on indefinitely? I do not think so. We are borrowing money now to pay part of the interest on what we owe. What be'comes of the mortgagee when he finds himself in that position? The end is not far off. I heard the ex-Minister of Finance state the other day that if future loans are needed-and they will be needed this year-they should be raised in Canada, rather than in a foreign country. That depends upon circumstances, in my judgment. If there is not a surplus of liquid capital in the country over and above what is necessary for the commercial and industrial life of the nation, over and above what the small borrower who cannot borrow outside the country is legitimately entitled to borrow-the man who wants to mortgage his farm, the village or town that wants to raise money on bonds, and numerous other .small borrowers who must borrow in the home market if they borrow at all-

The Budget-Mr. Hughes
if there is not a surplus over and above what is required for these purposes, to raise a loan in this country would (be to drive these borrowers out of business and dry up the sources of revenue. So, the government cannot borrow in the home market without regard to all the existing conditions; it must leave liquid capital enough in that market to carry on the industrial and commercial life of the nation, enough liquid capital for the small borrower who cannot obtain money elsewhere. The Government can go outside; but could our commitments abroad be made larger with safety to the nation? A few weeks ago when the Minister of Finance announced in this House that he had placed a loan of $100,000,000 in New York at a very favourable rate of interest there was considerable applause in the chamber. I did not applaud. Not that I was not pleased to know that Canada could borrow abroad at a fairly good rate of interest; but I felt sad that we were obliged to do so, sad that we were obliged to put a mortgage for another $100,000,000 on the old homeland; for that was really what we were doing. If we were borrowing and the money was used for purposes which would provide for the interest and a sinking fund it would be all right; but that $100,000,000 went to pay a debt already incurred and we are borrowing now to pay the interest on what we owe, or at all events borrowing to meet the ordinary expenditure of the country. That, in my judgment, cannot continue or certain results will follow. I suppose hon. gentlemen opposite-some of them at all events- would throw a fit at the mention of the word "annexation", but would the word "absorption" be more palatable or more agreeable to them? I will be quite frank in connection with this matter. I would not be afraid of the commercial results of such a policy, but I do not want the political results that would follow. Our political institutions, in my judgment, are far preferable to those of our neighbours; and it would be a sad ending, not only to ourselves, but perhaps to the world- to the English-speaking world at all events

if we could not maintain our political institutions. But hon. gentlemen who, a few weeks ago, clamoured for the expenditure of millions of dollars on non-productive services-on the army and navy; Who clamoured for the expenditure of millions of dollars in preparation for another war, were, in my opinion, taking the first step toward the extinction 
of our national life, though they look at it from another standpoint altogether.
I listened to, and I read very carefully, the speech delivered by the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), and I do not think it was worthy of him. In that speech, from beginning to end, I found no helpful thought nor suggestion. My hon. friend seemed to think that no responsibility rests upon him and the other members of parliament who, as has been stated by the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Johnston) were in office when this enormous debt was piled up upon the country. In that speech, from beginning to end, I could not find a suggestion where a new market for one dollar's worth of Canadian products could be discovered;
I could not find a suggestion as to where one additional acre of land could be put under tillage in Canada; I could not find a suggestion as to where one man, who is not now getting it, might receive employment; I could not find a suggestion where the revenues might be increased or greater economy practised. What was to be found in the hon. member's speech? Criticism of a petty character ending with a resolution which has been so very well described by my hon. friend from Last Mountain and so accurately designated by the Montreal Gazette, the sanest paper supporting the Opposition which I read. The characterization of the Montreal Gazette is worth quoting. It says:
The amendment recalls the couplet:
"You shall and you shan't,
You will and you won't;
You'll be damned if you do,
And you'll be damned if you don't."
The amendment has been truly named by the hon. member who has just taken his seat as a cheap political manoeuvre, and an attempt to embarrass the Progressives and to condemn the Government for not doing something which the Opposition themselves hold would be ruinous to the country if it were done. Such is the ex-Finance Minister's conception of his duty to Canada under these trying and difficult circumstances. The amendment was seconded by the leader of the Opposition. In its nature that amendment resembles the handiwork of the leader of the Opposition more than it does that of my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Finance, because the latter's style of speech is good natured, wherein he differs fundamentally from his leader who seems to have a grouch against the world.
Some of the members of the Progressive party who have spoken have made sug-

The Budget-Mr. Hughes
gestions, notably the hon. member for Stratheona (Mr. Warner). Let me say here that many of these hon. gentlemen appear to consider it to be their duty to help with the administration of the country and to make suggestions from time to time with that object in view. Perhaps the suggestions are not always the best that could be devised; but if a man is doing the best he can to discharge his duty to the country in the position in which he finds himself placed, such conduct will be far more effective than indulgence in petty criticism or the introduction of embarrassing resolutions. My hon. friend from Stratheona, I think, seemed to favour an increase in the income taxation. I have already alluded to that subject and, for the reason which I gave, I think it can be carried too far. I have taken a little trouble to look into the income taxation in Canada as compared with that of the United States, Great Britain, Australia and New Zealand, and I find it follows very closely the income taxation of the United States, where, I presume, the conditions are very much like our own. We do not follow closely the income taxation of Great Britain; Australia and New Zealand follow it to a greater extent than we do. Wherein does our system differ from that of Great Britain? Our income taxation is smaller on small incomes. It can easily be verified. I come now to the sales tax, which, I think, our Progressive friends will say is very bad. However, there are some features about it that they would commend. One feature is the fact that every penny so collected goes into the treasury. Another
(Mr. Hughes.]
commendable feature is that the extra amount raised under this proposed tax will not cost one extra cent to collect. It is simple and inexpensive and all goes into the treasury. That is a good feature of taxation. It may, it is true, bear more hardly on the man in moderate circumstances, or on the poor man with a large family, because his purchases will be larger in proportion to his means than the wealthy man's. But is there any system of taxation in the world that is perfect? There is not. Now, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) found himself in this position. He had an estimated revenue of $332,000,000, and he had to provide for an expenditure of perhaps $500,000,000. The actual expenditure last year was $496,000,000. He had. to close up the gap somehow. How was it to be done? We must have in this country, no matter what political party is in power-it would be necessary if the Progressives were in power-a customs taxation that will give the largest revenue possible. And after that we shall have all the taxes we can pay. The customs revenue now produces only about one-fifth of the total taxation. Where is the other four-fifths to come from? About two-fifths, I believe, is provided by the excise tax, the revenue from the post office, the inland revenue tax, the income tax, and so forth. And there is still two-fifths to be accounted for. Hon. gentlemen will therefore see the difficulties of the situation and the burdens and responsibilites that rest on the shoulders of any man who is at present, or who may be for many years to come, charged with the management of the finances of Canada. There are avenues of information open to the Minister of Finance and his officials that are closed to the ordinary citizen; and if we have a minister in whose integrity and honesty we have confidence, and of whose ability we are assured, we must trust him to a very large extent. There is no getting away from that.
The men who were in office when these enormous debts were incurred, and who now criticise the Minister of Finance for not doing better, seem to forget their responsibilities very quickly. I know that extravagance and waste are the concomitants of all wars. But there were expenditures during the late war that were premeditated extravagance, and I make this charge against the late government, that at all events they did very little to curtail those expenditures. They did not do all that they could have done, and every man in Canada knows that who is prepared to admit the facts.

The Budget-Mr. Hughes
For the condition in which we find ourselves to-day thgse men, I say, are responsible, to a large extent at any rate.
The hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Johnston), I might here remark in passing, said that there was no sales tax in the United States, but I see that a very influential body of financial men who met in New York quite recently were considering the advisability and the necessity of introducing such a tax there. They say that it cannot be done without. Some contend that it is the best kind of tax. I will not go so far as to say that, but I have advocated that tax in this House and I support it now for the reasons I have given. It is necessary in the exigencies of the situation. Where was the minister to turn to make up the loss of revenue from the income tax and the business profits tax? He has estimated that while these sources of revenue gave us some $100,000,000 last year, this year he will do very well if they bring in $60,000,000. The business men of Canada know that their profits have largely disappeared; and incomes have fallen. So that we cannot get from these sources the revenue we got last year, and the difference must be made up. I personally disapprove of borrowing, if it can possibly be avoided; and the revenue must be raised. I have already stated that we cannot economise beyond a certain point; if we do, we destroy the sources of revenue. The public business of the country must be carried on. Canada must develop or die. We are an undeveloped country, unlike Great Britain, France or the European countries that are fully developed. We have important public works to maintain and further works are required for the proper carrying on of the national business. These must be provided or we suffer the consequences. We must have a larger population, and in order to secure more people we must develop our railways. Now, in my judgment, it is the duty of those hon. gentlemen who object to the sales tax and other forms of taxation to suggest something better. How is the money to be raised?
A few days ago, speaking in this Chamber, the right hon. the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) twitted me a little and said that when certain things were taking place in the Parliament of Canada I was back in Prince Edward Island. I do not know what the right hon. gentleman meant by the word "back". It is quite true that from 1917 to 1922 I was not a member of this House, but a good majority of the electors of King's County,
Prince Edward Island, in the exercise of their constitutional rights, declared at that time that I ought to be a member of the House. The leader of the Opposition and those associated with him, however, in the blackest political crime ever committed in Canada or in any other Englishspeaking country, took care that I should not be a member of the House of Commons, and to make sure of this the constitutional rights of the people of King's County were violated. I say it is a political crime of the first magnitude to strike at the very foundation of the constitution. Sir, our constitution is based on the free, honest expression of the electors at the polls. Take that away and you take everything. The right hon. gentleman therefore knew why I was not a member of this House. And I wonder at his imprudence in reminding me of the fact. But apparently he is not sorry for the part that he and others that I can name took on that occasion. For myself, I would rather a thousand times have remained in Prince Edward Island than do what the right hon. gentleman and those associated with him did; I would rather remain in Prince Edward Island during the rest of my natural life than stand where he stands to-day. That is the reason.
_ Now, Mr. Speaker, I have presented the views that in my opinion should receive consideration from hon. members under present conditions, and having done so I feel that I have discharged the duty I owe to my country and to myself.

Mr. Speaker, as a new member I feel that I must join with those who have already expressed their appreciation of the manner in which the budget was presented by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). As to the substance of it, I may have views somewhat different from those held by some hon. members who have preceded me. Being as it were still a novice in this House, in rising to criticize the budget of such an experienced parliamentarian as the hon. Minister of Finance-who in the course of his public life has presented many budgets- I speak with some degree of trepidation; but I realize that it is my duty to express my views regarding the fiscal policy of this country, and I know that you will agree with me, Sir, when I say that in this budget is wrapp rd up our trade and fiscal policy. I have often heard it said of people who do not succeed well in business, although they and their employees and family seem to work very hard, that "there
2230	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Fansher '
is something wrong with the management". And I sometimes think that although we are a very industrious people we have not made the progress that we should have made in the decades that have passed since the inception of our so-called National Policy. Although I do not intend to lay all- the blame on our fiscal policy, I am thoroughly convinced that in a large measure that policy is responsible for conditions as we find them to-day. Of course, we all realize that prosperity cannot follow destruction, and we must make full allowance for the derangement of trade caused by the Great War. But I do claim that the fiscal policy we have pursued for the last thirty or forty years has caused an unequal balance in the development of industry. Right here I want to say that there is a growing demand for a change in our tariff policy. Indeed, there was already a growing demand for such a change prior to 1911, and although at that time there seemed to be a verdict rendered against tariff revision and better trade relations with the United States, yet I venture to say that had that issue been considered on its merits alone it would have had the overwhelming support of the electors.
In times past our tariff policy has not had that fair consideration at the hands of the electorate which it should have had, for always there have been injected into the issue other issues which were not relevant at all and which were introduced to obscure the real issue before the people This demand for tariff revision was still insistent after 1911, and even Sir Thomas White stated that such revision was long overdue. The country at large looked forward to the day when there should be a downward revision, but the Great War intervened, and domestic issues were laid aside in order that we might concentrate our efforts on the common purpose of bringing the war to a successful conclusion.
Shortly after the armistice it was considered advisable to have a revision of the tariff, and with that end in view we remember the appointment of a commission of which the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) was chairman. That commission went all over the Dominion taking evidence in regard to the tariff, and I wish that we had before us some of the information contained in the verbatim records of the hearings, for I am sure it would be very instructive to us. For instance, I recall a meeting in one of our Ontario cities at which a certain individual engaged
[Mr. Fansher. 1
in the manufacture of gloves was very urgent that the protection to his industry- 35 per cent-be maintained. The chairman asked the manufacturer where he procured his raw material, and he answered that his leather came from Brazil, his buttons from Concord, N.H., and certain other components from Italy and Turkey; in a word, all his raw material originated outside Canada. Yet he was asking that his protection of 35 per cent be maintained. The one and only thing that originated in Canada in connection with his gloves was the 'buttonhole.
Now, in contrast with a policy of that sort, I was pleased when it was stated in the budget speech that we should endeavour to encourage the inherent native industries of this country. In that regard I am heartily in accord with the sentiments expressed in the budget. But so far as the items of tariff reduction are concerned, I cannot see that much advance has been made in that direction. It is true that a reduction is made in the British preferential tariff; and with that I am thoroughly in accord. It is a policy which the Progressive party have always stood for, and which, in fact, is one of the planks in our platform. There has also been a slight reduction in the duties on agricultural implements-very slight, however, and offset, perhaps, largely by the sales tax. I admit that the Government have made some progress in the matter of the reduction of duties on agricultural implements, and I realize that if similar reductions were made yearly, in the course of five years a number of agricultural implements would be on the free list. But as I say, the sales tax largely takes away that apparent reduction. However, perhaps the sales tax is to be preferred to customs duties. The sales tax has one point in its favour: most of it is paid into the treasury of the country, whereas the customs tariff gives by way of protection two or three dollars in order to get one. In that respect I think the sales tax has some advantage over a customs tariff.
I want to deal briefly with some of the things which have been included in former budgets and might well, in my opinion, have been continued or revived in the budget of this year. An item which has been dealt with in previous budgets, for instance, and has been revived in this budget is the increased duty on automobiles. Those who were in this House a year ago will remember that the business profits

The Budget-Mr. Fansher
tax was dropped last year-a tax which did not become effective until after a certain percentage of profit on the money invested had been made. The investor was given a reasonable profit on his money, and certain percentages were collected by way of taxation as the profits grew. That tax brought in, during the five years that it was in operation, about $180,000,000; and there are some arrears to collect which may bring the total up to $200,000,000. When this tax was done away with last year, the sales tax was increased. I notice that no reference is made this year to the business profits tax or to its revival. It is said that this tax is now largely collected by the income tax. That may be true in some degree, but it is not wholly the case. The sales tax, as was pointed out to-day, is collected from the individual even if he has made no profit, even if he has sustained a loss of 10 or 15 per cent or more. On the other hand, as I have said, the business profits tax was not collected until after a reasonable profit had been made. In that connection I think there should have been a continuance of the business profits tax rather than an increase in the sales tax.
Now, in speaking on this budget I do not wish to be narrow in the views which I express. I believe that our national existence depends largely on our fiscal and trade policy. These must be such as to develop the inherent national resources of our country. We have had it made plain to us since this debate was opened that we have a large debt which, both as individuals and as a nation, we are in honour bound to discharge. I was somewhat surprised at the comment of the hon. member for King's, P.E.I., (Mr. Hughes) when he said that the only way to meet this deficit, the only way to discharge our debt, was by taxation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Taxation or borrowing. If that is the only method we can employ, we shall fall short of discharging our debt. How are debts paid? I am a farmer and I am going to give an illustration from the farm. If a farmer has debts to discharge he must apply himself to the digging out of that soil something that he can put on the markets of the world with a view to producing a return with which he can discharge his debt. His investment is in the soil; he must get the return on his investment. He must use the best business
powers that he possesses; he must sell in the best market that he can obtain; he must economize, and with the amount that he receives in excess of the cost of production and shipment to the markets of the world, he discharges his debt. The same is true of a nation; we shall never get out of debt by simply developing those industries which are not native, not inherent to this country-industries which derive their raw material largely from outside of this country, as well as a good many of the things necessary in the process of converting those raw products into finished products that are of value. For instance, we import steel and iron ore from outside of Canada, and we import the coal with which to convert it into the finished article. At the same time we have in this country raw materials which might well be developed within our own borders, thus resulting in the development of our own country rather than of other countries the industries of which draw their raw materials from sources outside of Canada.
For the last twenty years we have followed a system of assistance to certain privileged industries, running all the way from 5 to 10, 15, 25 and 35 per cent. We have certain industries to-day which have a protection of 35 per cent. Now, when an industry is protected to the extent of 20 or 30 per cent, it is evident that some one must do the assisting. The hon. member for Last Mountain said the tariff reductions were all right so far as they went, but they did not go far enough.
