If our manufacturers were seriously affected it would simply mean that a large number of workmen in Canada would be thrown out of employment.
The hon. member for Last Mountain said that three things were needed in Canada, the first of which, in his view, was immigration. Well, no doubt it is important that we have immigration, provided we have the right kind. I am not going to enter into the discussion of that subject now, or say anything about orientals, but it is exceedingly important that we get the right kind of people in Canada. The hon. member says that immigration will solve
the railway problem. Well, that is what the railways say, too. The Canadian Pacific Railway and other transportation companies think of nothing else but bringing more people into the country because they believe they can make money thereby. They advocate taking down the bars and letting everyone come in so as to build up the country. They want this in order that they may be able to pay dividends. That is all very well; but you have to think about the people who are here now. We must give them the first consideration. We have marching down to Ottawa now what is known as the McDonald Army of unemployed,,-returned men who are coming from Toronto to lay their claims before the Government for employment. What are we going to do for them? Our first consideration should be for the returned men; we must take care of them. In other parts of Canada there are returned men who are apparently in destitute circumstances. Last year in Vancouver one of the returned soldiers' clubs provided 3,000 men with clothing. This year there are as many more asking for clothing, and at the present time that association has advertisements in the newspapers asking that people who have winter clothing and other garments that they are now casting off should turn them over to the association in order that they may be given to those who are in need. Those are things to be taken into consideration. We ought first to provide employment for the men already in Canada before we think about bringing in others.
The hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Johnston) has intimated that he does not like the amendment; indeed, he suggests that it is a piece of " political trickery." That will be his reason, I presume, for voting against the amendment, because really he criticises the Government for not carrying out their pre-election tariff pledges. In his opinion the Government are entirely wrong in disregarding those pledges, and therefore the budget is unsatisfactory. At the same time he is going to vote against the amendment because it is a piece of " political trickery." Well, I do not think anyone would question the honour or integrity of either the mover or seconder of this amendment. Even during the campaign, when occasionally some rather bitter expressions were heard, so far as I am aware no charges of dishonourable conduct were levelled against the leader of the Opposition.

The Budget-Mr. McQuarrie
Let us examine the amendment and see if there is anything wrong with it. Does it contain any misstatement of fact? I suppose the hon. member for Last Mountain would have pointed out any such misstatement if he could, and his failure to do so may be taken as conclusive evidence that the terms of the amendment are correct. Therefore I submit that the amendment is a true statement of fact. The amendment recites part of the Liberal platform. I do not think any hon. member will take exception to the correctness of that recital. Then it is said that the Liberal party incorporated this platform in the official handbook which it issued. I do not suppose that will be denied, because the handbook speaks for itself. It is further stated that during the campaign the pledges contained in the platform were repeated on the hustings. I do not suppose that is disputed. It might have been added that in British Columbia, for instance, the Liberal candidates sent representatives around " on the side " to tell the people not to believe that the Liberal party was going to carry out its pledges, and to promise that there would be no free trade, no reciprocity, and no tariff reductions to any great extent. In confirmation of this those representatives said to the people in effect: You remember 1896? The Liberal party then made the same kind of promises, but when it came into power it forgot all about them. In any event I do not think that the accuracy of that part of the amendment can be disputed. The next paragraph is to the effect that the Liberal party having been returned to power does not carry out these pledges. Well, the hon. member for Last Mountain has criticized the Government for its failure to redeem these pledges. That statement, then, cannot be disputed. The last paragraph of the amendment states:
That the making of such solemn pledges, the utilization of them to secure support, and their flagrant violation after the attainment of office reveal a disregard of political honour and tend to lower the standard of public life.
If my hon. friend does not accept the accuracy of that statement, but, on the contrary, condemns this resolution as a piece of " political trickery ", then I wonder what are the standards of political honour of himself and of those who think as he does. I realize that all the hon. members who sit around him do not share his views, that there are members of his party who do think that our standard of political honour should be maintained. But my hon. friend

and those who agree with him in regard to this amendment say in effect: You should not call attention to little things such as broken political pledges or false pretenses; that is " political trickery ".

Mr. Speaker, I rise to make a few observations, and if I wander from the subject I hope you will be good enough to draw my attention to it. I have listened very patiently in the House to try and get the broadest viewpoint possible, and I find that there is something sadly wrong with our fair Dominion. I do not know how to express it better than by saying that we have a sick country. Now what is the trouble with our country? As I believe, it is this: Our trade seems to be sluggish. We do not seem to have a sufficient amount of trade to make times prosperous. Our factories seem to have stopped running, for some reason or other. We seem to have a discontented people generally, and on top of all that we have a large number of unemployed throughout the country.
I have spoken of Canada as a sick country, but I want to say that she has a wonderful constitution. Her constitution is made up of her natural resources, including agriculture. From my observation in the past I would say that her constitution has been sapped for years, and is still being sapped, and if it were not an exceptionally good constitution we would have been bankrupt before to-day. The people have realized that things have not been going just as they should, and they have been employing different doctors at different times. We had Doctor Conservative for a while, and Doctor Liberal for a while, and still the patient did not seem to improve. I do not know just what the trouble is, but it looks to me as though we did not have the right medicine. Both the doctors have been applying practically the sams treatment, and still the patient continues to go down. To my mind, we need a new kind of medicine. I do not know exactly what is wrong with the old one, unless it is that one of its ingredients, the fiscal policy, has become too old and has spoiled, poisoning the other ingredients. We cannot expect the Dominion to get better as long as we administer the same kind of medicine. We need a new fiscal policy it seems to me; and I would suggest that if we adopt a sound fiscal policy and in connection with it introduce economy-a concentrated solution of economy-and administered it in large doses we may entertain the hope of improving the conditions in this Dominion.
I have been somewhat disappointed in the amendment which has been moved by hon. gentlemen to my right. Not being familiar with parliamentary procedure, I had supposed that when an amendment was introduced it was for the purpose of offering a better solution for the existing difficulties than was contained in	the
motion.	But the amendment does not
appear to be of that character. At least it does not have that look to the ordinary man from the wayside, if I may use the expression. Yesterday I overheard some old parliamentarians talking on the subject and they declared that the amendment was not a sound one either from the point of view of the statesman or from the point of view of the politician. Personally, I cannot see that the amendment contains any suggestions for improvement. And yet I think there is considerable room for raising the standard of political morals which, in the past, has been such that the confidence of the people has been undermined to a large extent. I claim that if a higher standard of morals had been inaugurated long ago the people would not have lost confidence in the public administration to the extent they have done. It is a very unfortunate thing that so many of our citizens throughout the Dominion have such little faith in either of the two oldtime political parties. In fact sometimes it would almost seem as if they had not faith in the Progressive party. To such an extent does this loss of faith exist that a large proportion of the people will not take the trouble to cast their votes at election time. Undoubtedly there is a change coming; when one wrong-doer accuses another it is an evidence that he is in a rather tight corner, and we may look for a confession from the accuser soon.
The Budget-Mr. Milne

Economy has been talked of here, but actions, not words, are needed. Economy should be practised not only under the federal government, but it should be given effect to all along the line. We should expect economy from our provincial and our municipal governments, and the individual citizen should practise dt also. Perhaps the nearer we get to the individual the greater extravagance we find; but that does not alter the fact that we must have economy in high places as well as in low places. To use a homely expression the federal government should take the bit in its teeth and press forward along the path of economy. The members of the House without exception should go to the country and preach economy from every rostrum they can find-economy not only for the next year, but for many years to come. Only by adopting a policy of that kind can we bring Canada back to where she should be.
As I listened to the budget, and later read it over and reflected upon it, I could not help wondering what our tariff policy was based upon. They tell us that the tariff is needed for the purpose of raising money; but; in my reading I have become more bewildered than ever in the endeavour to find out what the real basis of our fiscal policy is and how the rates imposed against goods coming into the country were arrived at. I have a few examples under my hand which may illustrate my point without an undue amount of talking. We find that yarn, composed wholly or in part of wool, pays a 30 per cent duty; and that yarn spun from mohair and alpaca is admitted free of duty. Now, for the life of me I cannot see why such fabrics as mohair and alpaca should not pay a duty when the ordinary every day wool, such as our people are compelled to use, has to pay one. We find that glass cut for the use of manufacturers for photographic purposes comes in free of duty; whereas common window glass is taxed. We go on down the list and we find that flannels, plain, not fancy, pay 35 per cent, and shirts and drawers 35 per cent. A little further down the list we see that raw silk and silk from the cocoon imported for the manufacture of silk underwear is admitted free of duty. We further find that in the reductions that have been made there is a 5 per cent reduction on collars and cuffs, and a 21 per cent reduction on shirts. I wonder, Sir, if the collars and cuffs are for the benefit of the new agri-
cultural immigrants that are expected to arrive in Canada?
Let me, in a word or two, show the unfairness of the tariff as between the manufacturer and the farmer. Now, I have no grudge against the manufacturer, absolutely none. What I stand for, and what the country expects, is fair play; but we find that the farmer in getting machinery to produce real wealth-and production from the soil is the creation of wealth-has to pay an average tax of about 15 per cent on his machinery, while he has to sell his products in the open markets of the world. The manufacturer, on the other hand, in a great many cases gets his raw material free of duty. For example rattan for furniture and baby carriages comes in free. It is the same with raw rubber; and when a manufacturer turns out his finished product it is protected at a figure in the neighbourhood of 30 per cent. I ask you, is it fair that one industry should get its raw materials free of duty and be protected on its finished product, whilst the other pays a duty on the implements it uses in producing real wealth and has to sell its products on the open market?
Now I have a few observations to make about the sales tax. I am not going to worry you with a lot of figures, but I will give you a concrete example, and for the purposes of my illustration I will take hon. members of the house. The hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Lewis) who sits beside me states that he has seven children so that his family, reckoning his wife and himself, numbers nine. I have only one child and so in my home there are but three persons. I understand that the Prime Minister is unmarried, therefore there is only one person to represent his home. I ask you, is it fair that the hon. member for Swift Current should pay nine times as much in taxation as the Prime Minister does?

Is it fair that the hon. member for Swift Current should pay three times as much taxation as I am paying? I will readily concede that he is doing more for his country than I am and yet he has to pay three times as much in taxation as I have to pay. I put it to you whether such a system of taxation is fair.
Referring to the farmer, I always have to look after him, although I do not pretend to seek any special favour .for him. I obtained my figures from the re-

The Budget[DOT]-Mr. Milne
turns made for income tax from a farm containing 317 acres under cultivation. In that return I find that the farmer has made actual purchases in connection with his farm operation-his binder twine, lubricating oil, small repairs and so on-to the amount of $544, which would be termed general expense. He paid a sales tax on that amount. I look down the list, and I find that he has fourteen months' board charged for hired men. I assume that $10 a month would not perhaps be too much to add for the actual groceries purchased for the hired men. That would mean that, in order to maintain his hired help, he would have to spend $140 in actual purchases. A little further down on the list I find an item of $4,506 for farm machinery, and that did not include his automobile. We are allowed a depreciation of 10 per cent. I think most people who make a study of the situation will admit that this is a fair depreciation. If the machinery depreciates to that extent, he would actually have to invest each year $450 to keep his machinery up to standard. That makes a total actual investment, which the farmer would have to make on that farm in order to maintain it, of $1,131.60. He pays a sale tax on those purchases of, I believe, 41 per cent. That means that he would have to spend $51.92 on the actual necessities to carry on farming operations. That does not include any purchases for his own living or pleasure or anything like that, but that amount is actually paid in order to carry on his work on the farm.
Let us compare a business man, or an office man who has a salary of from three to six, or eight to ten thousand a year, with the farmer to whom I have referred. The business man goes to his office. He has his lead pencils, pens and stationery supplied. Which of the two men pays the more? Is it fair that the man who is actually creating the wealth from the soil should have to pay this tax of $50 for the privilege of farming? I am taking the average farmer. The average man who is at any kind of office work, clerical or otherwise, does not require the same investment and gets off practically free of the sales tax. Is that a fair method? Is this tariff a fair way of raising money or of taxing people?
They tell us at every turn that we must have money, and that if we increase the income tax to raise money we are going to drive people away. Surely there is not a man in our Dominion who would leave the country if we increased his
sales tax in order to remove the tax from some of the bare necessities of life. Personally, for the sake of the poorer people in our country, I should like to see a budget brought down saying that we are going to allow the women and children of this country to buy coarse woolen clothes without a tax, so that they can keep warm, and that we are going to allow them to have all the oatmeal, prunes, rice and so on, that they require without paying a tax. If we take off this tax, I may be asked, where are we going to get the money to make up the loss? Surely, there is not a citizen in this Dominion who is receiving a salary of over $2,000 who would not be willing to pay a little more from his income, in order to be of assistance to those poor people.
The question has been asked "why don't you get after the farmers and get more money out of them by the income tax?" I am not going to ask favors for the farmers. If the farmers are eligible for taxation, if tfiey are making enough money to be taxed, I say "go after them and take it out of them." We do not want any special privilege-absolutely none. But from my observation through the country in the East and through the prairies, the most prosperous districts I have seen turn out to be golf links or bowling greens. You ask where the money is to come from. Tell me where the money is and I will tell you where to go for it. There is absolutely no use in trying to bleed a stone. You say the sales tax is an invisible tax and people do not know anything about it. There is no question in the world that every five cents added to the cost of a pair of shoes is a burden to our poor people, and they can only stand so mu'ch. The money has to be raised, and we have to go where it is in order to get it.
I said in the opening that agriculture and our natural products were the foundation of our Dominion. I say-and I was convinced of it before I came here, and I have heard it a great many times since- that agriculture and our natural products are the mainstay of our country. We might as well try to put the weather vane on the top of this tower before it is finished as to try to stimulate our artificial industries before we solve the diffi-
9	p.m. culties that beset our natural industries. I say that the tariff is not a fair one. I want a tariff that will deal with and tax all classes of people and industries of the country in a fair way, and that is according to their ability to pay. I stand for the principle of a fair tax for all classes.

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth

The budget seems to me to be simply one more demonstration that there is no essential difference between the two old parties. Perhaps, if we look at the matter from the historical standpoint, we should hardly expect that there would be any great difference between the two. We remember that the old Conservative party arose originally as the political expression of the landed proprietors of Great Britain. Later on the Liberal party arose as the political expression of the rising trading classes of the towns, and still later, after the industrial developments, of the manufacturing class of Great Britain. And naturally there arose a conflict of interests between these two groups. The one, the agricultural proprietors, stood in those days for protection; they wished to be protected against the importation of free goods, especially wheat, from the outside. On the other hand, the trading classes wished to be enabled to go into all the world and trade freely, and that was the origin of the free trade policy of the Liberal party of Great Britain.
Here in this country the situation has been entirely different; and to a very considerable extent these old terms, " Liberal " and " Conservative, " have designated simply, as has been well recognized, two political groups which were not fundamentally different in .policy. It is quite true that the Liberal party has followed, more or less the traditions of the older Liberal party of Great Britain. And there are a few very honourable exceptions, of those who are still very firmly convinced that the Liberal principles are absolutely correct, and who try to do the impossible thing, of holding to those principles in an age when the original conditions that produced them have entirely passed away. But we find that it has happened several times in this country that when a Liberal government has succeeded a Conservative administration it was almost inevitably driven to adopt similar fiscal policies. In the past the great masses of the people were very largely without political expression. Of course, up until a hundred years ago in the Old Land, it was an unheard of thing that the ordinary rank and file of workers should have even a vote. The first man who attempted to propagate the idea that the ordinary people should have the franchise was haled before the courts and charged with sedition. Gradually the common people obtained the vote, but it was
	|
very slowly that they began to have any opportunity of giving expression to the needs of the rank and file. For a long time they could elect either Liberals or Conservatives, and that was all. In Canada it has been pretty nearly the same. It was only within the last few years that, for the first time, we had, among the agricultural workers in Canada, a certain number of people who understood that the agricultural interests were entirely different from those of the business classes, whether those classes called themselves Liberals or Conservatives. It is in even more recent years that the Labour people, who form a very considerable part of the population of this country, have begun to understand that it is necessary that they too should give political expression to their views, and to realize that their policies are entirely different from those of the business classes which are represented more or less by the Liberals and the Conservatives.
From our standpoint, as Labour people, it seems as if the budget which has been presented to Parliament places the financial interests of the country before those of the common people. I do not intend to enter upon any detailed criticism of the budget, but I want to emphasize the view that the sales tax is inherently vicious in principle. I fancy that the thoroughgoing members of the old Liberal school will agree with me that any tax levied in this way, which falls very largely on the consumers, is essentially vicious in principle. Now, we have 'had it stated within very recent days by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) that we are to have an immigration policy which will bring in large numbers of children from the Old Land. Personally I cannot approve of a policy which contemplates introducing into this country children gathered up more or less from the streets of the cities of the Old Country. I would suggest that we take a lesson from our farmer friends, who are very much more careful about the selection of their seed grain and their stock than we are about the selection of our human stock. But we are bringing in these children from the orphan homes of the Old Land, and at the selfsame time are continuing a policy that makes it impossible for a great many people in this country even to hope to have homes of their own where they can bring up their families.
Reference was made by the last speaker (Mr. Milne) to the fact that this tax bears most heavily on those who are trying to

rear families. Some of us know what it is to buy boots and clothing for children and to provide a family with the ordinary necessaries of life. It is becoming increasingly difficult, especially in the cities, for the ordinary labouring men, who compose a very large proportion of the population, to provide even the barest necessities. I am speaking not merely of those men that work with their hands. I think, as well, of the clerks in the shops and offices, and I think of our own civil servants, many of whom to-day are obtaining smaller wages than the amount which the Department of Labour says is essential for the maintenance of even a minimum standard of living. Some of our civil servants are receiving a smaller remuneration even than the amount paid in my own city of Winnipeg to those who are assisted by the relief department of the city. And yet, with that condition prevailing in this country, we are adding taxes that will have to be paid by these people who are drawing such meagre wages and who to-day are finding it the greatest struggle to make both ends meet. I suppose this fiscal policy is but a part of the whole policy of the present administration. There is nothing here that in any sense will provide for releasing the energies of the people and thus guarding against the unemployment that is so rampant. Rather, we have a reversal to the old policies with which we have been familiar for a great many years. It would seem very much as if the present administration were attempting to carry out the policy which the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway announced about a year ago when he said that it was absolutely essential that we should have a larger immigration to this country for two reasons:	First, that we
should have people who would help bear the burden of taxation; second, people who would help feed the railroads.
Now, that appears to be the policy of the present administration. They are bringing in people to help us bear our taxes-not a very kind policy for the immigrants-and to help feed the railroads. Surely that has been one of our policies for a great many years. The administration seems to be bankrupt in ideas and incapable of formulating any new policy that will really meet the situation with which we in Canada, in common with the people in many other countries, find ourselves confronted at tLfi present time.
There are no real economic changes proposed so far as I can see. It simply means that we are going to continue a principle which has been followed for a good many years, namely, that of drifting and financing by fresh borrowings. In our ordinary private business affairs if we have to borrow money to meet even the interest charges on sums already owing we think ourselves in a bad way; yet that is precisely what we as a nation have been doing for some years. There is a painting in the Canadian National Gallery by George Ag-new Reid, called "Mortgaging the Homestead." Some of us remember how in our earlier days it was considered to be one of the most serious steps that any family could take when it had to mortgage the old homestead. But I take it, Mr. Speaker, that that is precisely what we are doing as a nation: we are mortgaging the old home which our forefathers left to us.
Unfortunately we are mortgaging our home to no small extent to outsiders. Two years ago the Mining and Engineering Record gave the following figures with regard to the ownership of some of our great industries:
Americans control 95 per cent of the mining investments in Canada; 100 per cent of the pulp and paper investments in western Canada; 75 per cent of the lumher industries, and 75 per cent of the fisheries.
A few years ago all these industries belonged to Canada; to-day from 75 to 90 per cent of them are in the hands of foreign capitalists. On January 28, 1920, one of our western papers, the Winnipeg Free Press, stung by the fact that it could not obtain paper from an American company on terms which it thought equitable, printed the following editorial:
If there is money in it for the capitalist, ship our coal out of Canada to the highest bidder and let the Canadian people freeze; ship out our lumber and leave the people houseless; ship out our pulp and paper and leave them without newspapers, and so on all down the line. The fact that in all these cases the products are primarily the property of the people themselves would make no difference to the Gazette. On with the business of exploitation! The sacred system by which millionaires are turned overnight into multi-millionaires must not he tampered with.
The particular phrase to which I should like to call the attention of hon. members is that, "the products are primarily the property of the people." Yet they have been sacrificed in the interests of a comparatively small group. Let me quote from a publication recently issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce. The article

A significant feature of post-war development in Canada is the part played by the United States. The United States for many years past has entered into the development of Canadian resources, supplying both capital and labour and establishing industries on the Canadian side of the border. The nickle and asbestos production of Canada is largely in the hands of American companies. Many of her timber products and a proportion of pulp and paper production are also American. There are in all over six hundred United (States branch factories or subsidiaries in the Dominion, among which may be cited the International Nickel Company Limited, the Montreal Locomotive Works, Limited, the Canadian Consolidated Rubber Company Limited, the International Harvester Company, Limited, the Canadian General Electric Company, Limited, subsidiaries of the International Paper Company, the Ford Motor Company of Canada, Limited, General Motors, Limited, and the Stude'baker Corporation of Canada. Canada owes much to American initiative, capital and immigration.
There we have a statement as to how gradually American capital is coming^ in and gaining control of our great industries. The same is true with regard to stocks and bonds. Let me quote from the same publication:
Stocks, bonds and other securities held by incorporated and joint stock companies engaged in the manufacturing industries of Canada in 1918: Par values: total owned in Canada, $945,443,658; in Great Britain, $153,757,825 ; in the United States, $554,943,177 ; total in other countries, $17,221,322.
That is 34 per cent of all these stocks, bonds and securities are owned in the United States. Appended to this statement in this note:
When the compilation of 1920 figures is complete it may be found that the 34 per cent shown in the first table as the proportion held by United States capitalists in Canadian industries has increased to nearly 50 per cent, and that the British percentage has increased little or not at all.
One other quotation in this same connection, which goes into detail in regard to the ownership of the stocks and bonds of our industries. I shall quote only the percentages of these stocks and bonds owned by United States capitalists; they are as follows:
Lumber, 27 per cent; pulp and paper, 24 per cent: agricultural implements, 31 per cent; meat packing, 41 per cent; rubber, 50 per cent; patent or proprietary medicines, 86 per cent; automobiles, 61 per cent; car construction, 59 per cent; artificial abrasives, 99 per cent; automobile accessories, 93 per cent; brass and copper castings, 44 per cent, and so on all down the line.
We may say that we own, or that Great Britain owns this country, but I submit,

Mr Speaker, that if our natural resources are owned by great American companies, and our stocks and bonds by American syndicates, our ownership is a very empty possession. I may claim to own a house, but if that house is mortgaged for almost its entire value, my ownership is a very empty thing indeed. A good many of us are reduced to the position where we have to turn over the greater part of our income to the men who hold the mortgages; and it would seem as if in Canada we are rapidly coming to that position where we have to turn over a very considerable amount of our national income to people who live outside of this country. The latest loan placed would seem to be no exception to this rule. We had to negotiate a loan of $100,000,000 on the other side of the line, which simply means that we shall continue to pay interest across the way. If a Canadian should manage to acquire some part of that loan, as long as he remains in Canada he is taxed, but if he establishes a residence in the United States he will, apparently, be free from taxation. That is a point which I hope will be discussed when we come to that particular item.
But I would suggest that not all the mortgages are held outside of Canada. There has been in the past few years a remarkable shifting of the wealth of this country from a large group to a comparatively small group. I wonder if I may be permitted very briefly to run through some of the outstanding stages in the history of this country by which our lands and publie resources have been gradually alienated. We remember that when our forefathers came to Canada and carved out for themselves homes here, the whole of this land was owned by the Crown. Possibly we might make exception and admit that there were certain trading rights conceded to the Hudson's Bay Company and that to that extent a private organization had a sort of mortgage on the country. But on the whole, all our resources were publicly owned; and had our policy been a true one, those resources and the organizations which have been built up upon them would still remain in the hands of the public. But what have we done? In the first place, the earlier fur traders exploited the Indians and out of the money they made were able to acquire other natural resources in this country. We all remember the earlier ecclesiastical and feudal grants which were made. It may seem unneces-

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
sary to review past history, but when we come to study some of the older cities in this country, we find that the present landlords are the successors of those who acquired lands in this way from the Crown in the early days. This was under the French regime. Then, under British rule, there came the granting of huge tracts of land. Lord Dufferin stated that in Ontario almost one-half of the lands then surveyed had been given away. In Quebec over half the lands were given away, and so with the other older provinces. It is not my purpose to enter into a discussion of the alienation of lands as clergy reserves and under the administration of the Family Compact, and, later, the giving of huge blocks of land in the settlement of the Hudson's Bay Company's claims. Why do I recall this past history? Because I would like to show, if I could, that the earlier fortunes of Canada were gained out of the fur trade, out of the grants of Crown lands to the pioneer settlers, and that in this way these resources which ought to have been held in trust for the whole of the people have been secured by a very few of the people.
Then, after that earlier pioneer period, our railway systems began to develop, and we have again the building up of huge fortunes. It would be a comparatively easy thing to enumerate the shareholders or directors or promoters of these earlier railway companies; in a very great number of instances the men who are prominent in our industrial and financial affairs of to-day are descendants of the men who made their fortunes by securing lands and other resources from this country without giving the community any equivalent. I am going to venture to quote a paragraph from David Mills which, illustrates the reckless way in which our franchises were given away in those early days:
"Corruption taints the majority of railway enterprises from their inception to completion," wrote David Mills, a member of the Dominion Parliament, and later Dominion Minister of the Interior. "Charters are sought, not infrequently, for the purposes of speculation. Sometimes they are used to blackmail existing railway lines. However much a railway road is needed, a charter is seldom obtained without difficulty, and stock is bestowed for parliamentary support. The names of wellknown railway men are sought to give credit to the projected enterprise, a number of shares are tendered them for their 'eminent services', and they are seldom declined.
"When a railway scheme is finally launched, it finds a large number of friends-engineers and professional contractors, the owners of rolling mills, and the builders of cars and loeo-

motives. The getters of land grants, and the traders in railway stocks, all come to its aid, and it may be, experience its bounty. These constitute the grand army of a private railway enterprise.
"Besides these, there is a numerous band of camp followers, who expect in a variety of ways 'to reap where they have not sown', but about whose special services nothing need be said. It is this numerous host of allies and followers which ' can kill or keep alive ' a railway project, and because they have this power, must be paid, that add to the cost of every rival railway undertaking." In his article Mills but stated a further well-known faot when he wrote: " In order to pay interest upon bonds or dividends upon stocks, a road is allowed to deteriorate. Then come accidents, in which scores of passengers are mangled or scalded."
That was the beginning of our railway enterprise; thus we had built these earlier lines which were afterwards incorporated into the great transcontinental systems. I do not need to read at length from tlhe Drayton-Acworth report, but you will remember the immense sums which were given to the privately owned roads. We have been almost staggered during recent weeks in hearing about the enormous amounts which it will be necessary for us to raise in order to carry on our publicly owned railroads. We must not forget the way in which these huge debts were incurred; we must not forget the enormous grants which have been made by this country right along to construct our railroads. The total public assistance direct or indirect, to the Canadian Northern amounted, according to the Drayton-Acworth report, to $298,253,263. To the Canadian Pacific there were enormous grants, as well as to the Grand Trunk and to the Grand Trunk Pacific-and land grants as well. The people of Canada through their government have provided or guaranteed the payment of sums totalling $968,451,737-almost a billion dollars, and upon these huge sums we are asked to-day to pay interest. You may say: Very well; this is past history; we have to start from the beginning. But we cannot start from the beginning; we have no right to start from the beginning. If you really want to go to the beginning, you have to go back to the time when this country was free. In Great Britain you remember there came at one period of her history the enclosure of the common lands, one of the most outrageous proceedings in the history of any country-when certain descendants of the feudal lords who had previously recognized certain responsibilities respecting the rights of their peasant population undertook to fence these lands which had been regarded as common lands

and to appropriate them and their revenue for their own purposes. We have had in Canada, this new, young country of ours, a much more outrageous proceeding than that of the alienation of the common lands cf Great Britain. We have had "the alienation of millions upon millions of acres of land and of the most valuable natural resources of this country, so that to-day the greater part of these are in the hands of private individuals, and now we are told that the public has no claim upon them. I need not go into the more recent alienation of our public resources. During the last few years I have been living more or less in British Columbia, and any one who knows the conditions there knows how recklessly our natural resources of timber and mines have been forfeited in that province, so that to-day the people practically have no control either of the better agricultural districts or of the mining or timbering properties.
We find here, referring again to the pamphlet which I have already quoted, issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce, a note with regard to the expansion of industry in this country:
The day of the manufacturer had dawned, and in 1912 the future of Canadian industry was looming large. The growth of the domestic market demanded expansion of domestic manufactures, but this expansion went further and made itself felt in greatly increased export.
Here again the people in Canada and their welfare was sacrificed in the interest of the larger manufacturers who were benefiting by these exports. The document proceeds:
The era of large business had begun and merger succeeded merger, with resultant increase in production. Industrial capital increased rapidly, from $445,000,000 in 1900 it rose to $1,247,000,000 in 1910 ; to nearly $2,000,000,000 in 1915, and to $2,787,000,000 in 1917.
Let me ask where did all this great amount of money come from? It came out of the primary producers of this country. There was no other place from which it could come; matters were so arranged that the greater part of this property was acquired by a few individuals. We find that instead of the numbers of establishments increasing, they decreased proportionately. In 1900 there were some 14,650 firms that produced a product valued at $481,053,375. By 1915 there were hardly a thousand more firms, but the value of the product had increased to $1,381,547,225.
We all know without my entering into a discussion of it how in connection with these mergers which have been going on in

recent years, there has been considerable of the process which is commonly known as watering stock. We all know how in recent years enormous fortunes have been made out of the rise in real estate values, and we know that these values, which are essentially community values, have gone into the hands of comparatively small groups, and that these enhanced values and this over-capitalization remains a perpetual mortgage on the productive industries of the country.
I can go on to show how gradually our financial organizations have been concentrated. Take, for instance, the banks. According to the statement issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce, we had 18 banks having total assets of $3,091,500,000. I suppose there are only 17 of these banks to-day, but they have these enormous assets. Next in financial importance to the chartered banks are the trust companies, of which there are about 25, either independent in operation or affiliated with one or other of the chartered banks. Their operations do not conflict with legitimate banking as they are almost wholly confined to trusteeship and the management of estates. Few of us perhaps except the financiers themselves realize just how far the banks really control the industrial concerns of the country to-day. As an illustration of this, let me take the grain trade in which a good many members of this House are more or less directly interested. I quote a paragraph from the report of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange for this past year, 1921:	[DOT]
Owing to the immense volume of grain marketed, and to the fact that practically all of the business is done on credit, banks have a primary interest in the system of marketing. Not many grain merchants or companies have sufficient capital of their own with which to do a large volume of business.
Let me say in passing that this throws a very important light on the real reason why the farmers of this country are asking for a wheat board. To continue:
All of them have to borrow large sums of money from the banks, or have large lines of credit, to enable them to do business. It is not generally realized that from the moment the farmer sells his wagon-load of wheat, or gets an advance upon it, the wheat is virtually owned by the banks. Indeed, one might go further and say that from the moment the farmer parts with his wheat at the local shipping point, the banks become the owners of it, and the banks remain the owners of it until it is eaten as bread by the consumers. Elevator companies, track buyers, commission merchants, shippers, exporters, mills and bakers are financed by banks, and in their relation to the

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
grain they are not much more than the agents of the banks that finance them.
That is the point that we must consider here. The capital of this country has become very highly centralized, and this high degree of centralization gives the financial institutions practically the control not only of the commercial and industrial enterprise of this country, but indirectly, of the very life of the labour people of this country.
Now let me go on to the later forms by which the people of this country have been exploited. I come to the war itself. We all know that some fortunes were made even during the South African war, but when we come to the Great War, there was never a more magnificent opportunity for the profiteer. It is not my purpose tonight to say anything with regard to the war contracts scandals* I think that they are fresh in the memory of any man who has ever attended a political meeting during the last few years in this country. We know the huge fortunes which were made during the war time. We know from the revelations which were given to this country by the Committee on the High Cost of Living how certain individuals and corporations were enabled to profiteer even during the time that their fellow citizens were laying down their lives in France. We know that these fortunes were made. Some of them, perhaps, have been sacrificed since; others of them are still held, and there has been no effort made by the incoming government, so far as I can see, to recover from the profiteers that blood money which they laid up during the time of the war. That has been -a great disappointment to some of us, because we recognize the opportunities that were granted to the incoming administration. What happened during the war? The administration of that time made it comparatively easy for men to make large sums. Professor O. D. Skelton, of the Department of Economics at Queen's University, is responsible for the statement made towards the close of the war:
In the four years of war Canada has met only 6 per cent of the direct principal cost of the war out of surplus revenue, as against 20 per cent met by the United Kingdom, while the United States has met the extraordinary proportion of 44 per cent the first year.
Then as to the incidence of taxation, Profesor Skelton shows that in the United Kingdom 81 per cent of the taxes were paid on property and income, and only 19 per cent on consumption. What was the condition in Canada? In 1913-14, nothing in the form of taxation on property and
income; 100 per cent paid out of consumption. In 1914-15 nothing paid on property and income; 100 per cent out of consumption. In 1915-16, 1 per cent on property and income; 99 per cent on consumption. In
1916-	17, 8 per cent on property and income; 92 per cent on consumption. In
1917-	18, 11 per cent on property and income and 89 per cent on consumption. Great Britain is said to be a conservative country owing to the fact that she has such a considerable part of her population who are property owners and who have large fixed incomes; and yet in Great Britain, 81 per cent of the taxes were taken out of property and income, while in Canada, and that only in the last year of the war, 11 per cent of the taxes came out of property and income.
How did we do our war financing? We borrowed and we borrowed more instead of paying as we went as we might have done-for it is a well known truth of economics that we as a nation produce every year almost as much as we consume-we went through the financial jugglery, known as "borrowing". The food, and clothing and ammunition which was needed during the war was produced during the war. The high financing which we did at that time was, after all, a matter of book-keeping by which a comparatively limited group of people obtained a strangle hold on the rest of the country. I think I may obtain confirmation of my statement on this point from a pamphlet issued by the right hon. Sir Thomas White, Minister of Finance from 1911 to 1919 entitled "The Story of Canada's War Finance". I quote two short paragraphs:
This view overlooks the fact that our War Loans were really subscribed by the public from the savings made during the War itself. There is real truth in the statement that was made frequently by economists that nations pay for Wars as they go along. Productive enterprise is, of necessity, greatly stimulated. This, coupled with the constantly increasing rise in wages and in the prices of commodities, produces an enormous amount of credit, or money so called, which finds its way into the pockets and the savings accounts of the public. This money is available for subscriptions to government loans. On the other side of the national account is the vastly increased public debt representing the money expended for the equipment of the nation's forces, the food consumed by them during the course of the War, and the immense amount of ammunition used in the field. The burden of the debt created is passed on to future generations as a legacy and reminder of the waste of war.
And again:
From the national standpoint, it is of the utmost advantage that so large a proportion of

our War Debt is held by the Canadian people themselves. I hesitate to think ot what our position would be if we had borrowed, and were still owing', externally, even half the amount of our war debt. We should be kept in economic servitude through adverse exchange for a generation to come.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to comment briefly on this passage which I believe is sound economics. Sir Thomas confesses that nations pay for wars as they go along. He confesses that our war loans were really subscribed by the public from the savings made during the war itself. Now, here is the situation which we have to face: We were told that the whole of this people ought to throw itself into the great war. We were told in those days that there ought to be equality of sacrifice. - Certain men went over to the front and lost their lives. Others went and gave the very best of their livei. Others stayed at home and put forth their best endeavours for the national welfare at that time; and on the other hand a small proportion of the population stayed at home and made hay while the sun shone-they coined money while their brothers sacrificed. The money that was "made" and put into war loans was made out of the war itself-let that sink into the minds of the people of this country-and we to-day have the right to say whether those people shall, or shall not, retain their ill-gotten gains. I think of some of the men who have returned from the front broken in health, broken in fortune. I think of several hundred of them who are reported to be marching on Ottawa at the present time in the hope that they will be able to present their case to this House. Have these men no claim upon the resources of this country? By the very budget that has been presented to us at this time those men, every time they buy a pair of shoes, or a coat, or a shirt to wear and every time they attempt to support any dependents that they may have, are asked to contribute still further to that war. And where does their money go? The greater part of their money, paid through taxes, goes to the very people who profiteered at the time they were fighting in France. I for one cannot conceive that the returned men across this country are going to tolerate that condition of things very much longer. Sir Thomas White says that it is a splendid thing that this money is not owed to people outside of Canada- that it is owed to the people in Canada. From my standpoint-and I think I can speak for a very large number of the common people of this country,-it does not make very much difference whether 
the money is held by some great corporations in this country or outside, or by wealthy people in this country or outside, the fact is that the poorer people of Canada are compelled to pay interest on these war loans to others who have not, up to the present, been required to make anything like an equality of sacrifice.
In an article published on April 1st in Maclean's Magazine the writer, Mr. John A. Stevenson, calls attention to the enormous burdens which we have placed upon our shoulders in this country, not merely by the federal taxation, but by this taxation, supplemented by provincial and municipal taxation. He has estimated that the federal taxation amounts to $435,000,000, the provincial taxation to $90,000,000, the municipal taxation to $350,000,000, a total of $875,000,000. That means that we have a taxation burden in this country of $100 per head, or, taking a family of five, which is not a very high average, we have a taxation burden of $500 per family. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that we shall have to face in the near future the ultimate and final solution of these huge debts which we have accumulated. Personally, I can see nothing for it but repudiation or a capital levy. Some people do not like that word "repudiation." In the case of those who own large fortunes which were made during the war, I take it that it would be a highly just thing to repudiate. It would simply be the country taking back what the country ought never to have given away or allowed to be taken away. We do not call it repudiation when a man has stolen a large amount and the state comes along and takes it back. I recognize of course the practical difficulty that a certain amount of this money has shifted from one person to another, and that we cannot very well, in all cases at least, lay our hands on the war profiteers, but we can place our hands on those who, to-day, have the ability to give, and a just system of taxation surely ought to be placed on ability to pay. In Great Britain they are already advocating a capital levy. That simply means an extension of the present principle of taxation. It has long been recognized as the right of the state to step in and tax. The income tax is a recognition that the state may take a certain percentage of the income. We have heard a good deal in Canada about what splendid people the labour people in Great Britain are, and how constructive they are in their policies. Let me remind hon. members that in the draft programme prepared several

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
years ago for the British Labour party it was suggested that the income tax should begin at 1 shilling in the pound and rise to 19 shillings in the pound. This afternoon some figures were quoted that showed that in the case of very large incomes the taxation already amounted to almost half the income. Great Britain-Conservative old Great Britain, as we sometimes call that country-has gone a great deal further than we have in taxing large incomes. We have gone a very small distance in succession dues, in inheritance tax. Why should we allow large fortunes to be passed on by one individual to his heirs? We all recognize the responsibility of a man to provide as well as he may for his immediate dependents, and arrangements could very well be made by which dependents could be provided for up to a certain amount, but I think it is generally conceded that it is no kindness to the heirs to leave them huge fortunes. As far as the public is concerned, since the individual does not pass on the food and clothing to his children, it simply means that, in some way, he passes on to his children the right to collect food and clothing and other necessities and comforts of life from the rest of the community. That is, he passes on to his children a mortgage which the rest of the community has to pay. We shall at some time have to recognize that no man has the right to mortgage a generation as yet unborn. That is precisely what we are doing in allowing huge fortunes to be passed on, as we have done and are doing.
Before passing away from the war loans, I desire to point out another inherent evil of the system. We have been depending on certain standards of value which are not constant. While the war was on and the people obtained their loans, a hundred dollars represented, we will say, 50 bushels of wheat. A hundred dollars to-day, we will say, represents 100 bushels of wheat. This simply means that not only are those war loans free of taxation, but they have to be paid twice over. Is that a proposition which we are willing to accept for ourselves and our children? Sooner or later we must recognize that we are coming almost to a standstill in our industrial enterprises. Our railroads and our banks claim the right to their dividends. People engaged in industries say they cannot get along without their profits. On the other hand, we have an ever increas-
10	p.m. ing number of people on the very verge of starvation. Unless we can in some way alter the system, or introduce another system in its place, we are going to see tens of thousands of our fellow-citizens going down and under. I submit that the Government exists to provide for the needs of the people, and when it comes to a choice between profits and property rights on one hand and human welfare on the other, there should be no hesitation whatever in saying that we are going to place the human welfare consideration first, and let property rights and financial interests fare as best they may. That is the only position we can consistently take. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) in closing his remarks the other day made reference to labour and he said:
If labour at times seems to be unreasonable, let us not forget that in the days that have gone, too often the workingman, so called, did not receive a fair share of the wealth which his labour created; too often he saw his employer grow rich and prosperous while the workingman had little more than an existence. There has been a happy change in this respect.
I would like to ask, on behalf of the working man, when this change came about. At the present moment, with nearly 200,000 men out of work, and with some millions, presumably, of dependents involved in this unemployment, is the working man to-day getting much more than a mere subsistence? I speak not merely on behalf of <the manual workers, but on behalf of others who are receiving wages, and the lower paid salaried men. Are they getting much more than a mere subsistence? They cannot get anything else, unless we make fundamental economic changes. The Minister of Finance goes on to say:
But he has duties to perform. Labour has come to a sense of its power. Has it come to a sense of the responsibility and duty which should always accompany power?
Has Labour come to a sense of its power? Well, so long as there are two representatives in this House out of 235 members, I do not think it can be contended that Labour has come to a sense of its political power. When it does there will be a different kind of budget, I can promise you that. When we consider that Labour, of hand and brain, in shop and in office, composes a great proportion of the population of the country, we must recognize that it has not come to a sense of political power; and when we consider the state of labour organizations from coast to coast we cannot very well say that Labour has come into economic power. Rather the position has already come about which was referred to

The Budget-Mr. Baldwin
by Sir Thomas White. He said that if we owed these huge sums to people outside of the Dominion we should be kept in economic servitude for a generation to come. I submit that even although we owe the money to people in Canada the great majority of the people in this country are still subject to what can properly be termed "economic servitude." That is the thing we have to face. There is no use expressing pious wishes that Capital and Labour should get together unless we also say on what basis they are to do so. If the Minister of Finance says that they must come together on the basis of dividends for the railroads, of interest and dividends for the banks, and of big profits for the manufacturing concerns, while the labouring men of the country are on the verge of starvation, then I say Labour and Capital can never come together. I do not like to personify Capital, because it is so impersonal a thing, while the labourer is a creature of flesh and blood. But if those who represent Capital, on the one hand, and the labouring classes, on the other, are to get together with a view to solving the labour and social problems of the country, we must first of all see to it that there are certain minimum standards involving proper conditions of livelihood for every man and woman and child in the country. And until every man, woman and child is so provided for we ought not to talk further about profits and dividends. Before we can get our labour and social problems solved the great mass of the people must have, what they have not to-day, a real voice in the control of their own affairs and of the affairs of the country. Mr. Speaker, I cannot believe that any government, Liberal or 'Conservative, is going to be able to carry on very much longer in this country and put forward budgets such as that which has been presented by the present administration.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If the concluding remarks of the last speaker, Mr. Woodsworth, were true, it would indeed be a gloomy day in Canada. But the debate, so far as it has gone, seems to me to reflect a spirit of optimism. We know that an appalling debt has been piled up, particularly during the war period, and as stated by the hon. member for King's (Mr. Hughes) in his lucid remarks this afternoon, we must be taxed to the limit to discharge that debt. The worst feature of the situation is that the debt is growing, and I presume that this is what is creating 
a feeling of despondency on the part of certain hon. members. But the debate is not marked by the same acrimonious spirit that formerly prevailed, and censure is not indulged into so great an extent as was the case in years gone by. The situation calls for the serious thought of everyone, and there is not so great a tendency to indulge in political fighting. No one charges the late government with misconduct, and I will go no further than to say that they made serious mistakes. They certainly made a grave blunder in lending money to European countries that were not solvent; and they made a mistake in allowing the Food Control Board to continue the embargo on sugar, with the result that the people suffered to the extent of some $30,000,000; because the consumers had to pay in the long run. We have had the distinction for more than twenty-five years of having cheaper sugar in Canada than in the United States, and all these things count in the problem of retaining population. The hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Johnston) complains that we have not held the immigrants that have come into the country in the past decade. Well, the best way of holding not only immigrants, but the people who are already in the country, is to make the country a cheap place to live in, and if the Food Control Board had lifted the embargo on sugar eighteen or twenty months ago, an enormous quantity of refined sugar would have gone to the United States at 17 to 20 cents per pound, and when it was all gone we would have started on the level and sugar would have been as cheap here as in the United States. Another great mistake the government made was in taking over the railways, an action which even newspapers that always supported the Conservative party condemned. However, we have the railways on our hands now and we must give them a trial. But I see the cloud lifting on the horizon. I notice that there is a 10 per cent reduction being made in the freight rates in the United States as from the first of July, and from four to six millions will be saved in the pay list, beginning from the same date. We have imitated the United States in many ways that were not advisable, but I hope we shall be able to follow their example in this regard. The hon. member for Yale (Mr. MacKelvie), whose remarks I have been reading in Hansard, says that the Liberal party has not consistently adhered to any principle. Let us see what we have done. We promised the people of the country during the election that econo-

The Budget-Mr. Baldwin
mies would be practised in every possible direction; and I said in my own constituency that if the party I supported were returned to power and should spend one dime where the preceding government spent a dollar, I would	condemn
them.	Now the Opposition on the
25th day of April and on every day succeeding, when the militia estimates were brought into the House, beat the drums and put up various speakers in order to have those estimates increased. One of their speakers was the late mayor of Toronto (Mr Church), who had a good deal to say about the navy.
Let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, that after the great Disarmament Conference in Washington the United States reduced their naval and military establishments by many thousands of men and stopped construction of several great super dreadnaughts. General Bliss of the United States army, said that if we had another war that approached the last in expenditure of money and loss of lives the united churches of the world would be to blame. Some,one asked him why did he not so advise the President and Congress. He replied, "It is absolutely useless. Public sentiment must be aroused or nothing will be done to prevent another war. All the military men are keen on military training, and they are supported by the profiteers, who are great in number and possessed of vast wealth." Senator Lodge and other prominent public men of the United States have all declared that war is simply slaughter and destruction. Hon. members who favour a big navy and a strong militia force appear to imagine that there is an enemy behind every tree. Therefore, they say, "We must keep up a great war machine." They are absolutely wrong.
What does Canada want a navy for? The only useful purpose that a navy could serve, it seems to me, would be to destroy the icebergs that float down into the traffic lanes of the Atlantic. If by some invention our navy could perform that great service much valuable property and many precious lives would be saved. The United States are our friends, and they have the Monroe Doctrine. Let us remember that. We do not wish to be cowardly, but we do know that no nation upon the face of the earth would dare question the Monroe Doctrine. The United States would not let any nation invade Canada.

speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There is a smile on the faces of my friends opposite. I hate to
make any comparison between Canada and the United States, but suppose our neighbours should take umbrage and invade this country? In spite of everything we could do, it seems to me they would cut us into about three divisions, and they could do so without making any great effort or spending very much time about it. Some hon. members of the Opposition may say, "The member for Stanstead is a pussyfooted, sissified fellow." I want to tell them that there is not a man in this House who would use cold steel and cold lead quicker than I would to put down riots or rebellion after the Riot Act had been read and ignored. But we do not need a great army for police purposes. There is no better army or constabulary in any country than a happy, contented people. I do not believe in the great labour piasses of Canada depending on somebody else. I believe in their using their own ingenuity and industry and becoming honie-builders, if it means only a little ten by twelve house on a small piece of land. Those are the people who will uphold law and order, and in this great country there is nobody so poor but should be able to own a piece of land in our rural districts.
It has been said that the twentieth century belongs to Canada. We believe it. For the first decade of this century Canada's career was great and glorious, but then the war came and she got a blow in the solar plexus that paralyzed her. She is rapidly recovering, however, and if we only buckle down and do things this great Dominion will soon regain her former prosperity. It seems to me that we are now in a position somewhat analogous to that of the United States at the end of the Civil War. The people of that country allowed their military machine to go to pieces and set to work to develop their natural resources, and in two decades many of her veterans were wealthy men. We have to follow their example-get to work and develop our natural resources. We should be able to find employment for all our people, and as soon as we get them employed I would empty our gaols and penitentiaries, for I would not feed a single able-bodied prisoner while there was work for him to do in helping develop this great Dominion. As a Canadian I am optimistic. We have wonderful resources. Take our great waterways-the St. Lawrence system, the Great Lakes-and consider their potentialities. Think of the possibilities of the immense resources of which the Assiniboia and Saskatchewan rivers, flowing to the

The Budget-Mr. Baldwin
foothills of the Rockies, are the centre. But these resources cannot be developed in a day; in three or four decades, when the century is half gone, Canada may have a population of fifty millions, while the United States will certainly have two hundred and fifty million people. We have to do big things in this country; we are a vigorous people and we must have an optimistic outlook. It seems to me that we can have a great waterway system from the St. Lawrence and the Great Lakes to the foothills of the Rockies-to the province of Alberta at least; and in my opinion nothing would more surely cement the different provinces together; nothing would make their union more certain.
These geographical differences bring me to this thought, in passing: there has been some difference of opinion on the question of oleomargarine. When I went recently to my constituency I was asked how it was that the farmers in the House voted in favour of the importation and manufacture of oleomargarine, while others who were not farmers voted against it. Well, it is a question of geographical differences. It may happen that some of our hon. friends are not dairymen; and perhaps that is why we differ on these subjects. It is a matter of one taking one point of view, and one another.
The ex-Finance Minister (Sir Henry Drayton) has criticised the present Minister of Finance with respect to promises. Now, it was stated by a prominent member of the Conservative party-I myself heard him say it many years ago-that elections were not won by prayers. But I would remind my hon. friends of the Opposition that Sir John Macdonald had always proclaimed his policy as protection and reciprocity in natural products. That policy was proclaimed up and down the country from 1878; I myself heard it enunciated. And I hay say that if Sir Wilfrid Laurier had not been defeated in 1911 we would not to-day be worrying about the small population of Canada. In September, 1911, large numbers of persons had located lands in the West and were prepared to invest their capital in this country in the event of reciprocity being adopted. But when the result of the election became known they packed their bags and returned to the United States without making any further investments-and I say that they had been cautious enough not to invest very much before the result of the election became known. The ex-Minister of Fin-
[Mr Baldwin.]
ance, therefore, in censuring the present Minister of Finance has charged the members of the Liberal party with doing something of which his own party is guilty.
In connection with the criticisms of the ex-Minister of Finance, I may point out that it was he who, when Sir Thomas White found it necessary to retire, took the burden of the portfolio of finance upon his shoulders; and when he came to the House with his taxation proposals, there were more criticisms of his budget from his own side of the House than there were from any other quarter. It can easily be seen that the present minister is not in any such unfortunate position. The ex-Minister of Finance, on the occasion to which I referred, tinkered with his schedules and changed them from time to time until he got them into some kind of shape. I know that in the present budget no one is unfairly dealt with, but I am sure that the minister will be pleased to correct anything that is pointed out to him in that line.
There is but one way for Canada to develop, and that is to impress the sons and daughters of this country with the fact that it is a fine place to live in and that their prospects here are better than they would be in the United States. When young men ask me for advice on this subject I tell them that there are ten or fifteen chances in Canada to one in the United States, for them to be successful. I tell them that if they go to the United States they stand a chance of being servants only, whereas if they stay in Canada they can be their own masters and be amply repaid for their efforts.
The old province of	Quebec, the
greatest province of the greatest dominion on earth, was at one time deeply in debt, and it succeeded in getting out of that debt not by ousting one government and putting in another, but by the administration of affairs on a sound business basis. The result is that we are developing our great resources; we are making the forces of nature the servants of mankind. We are developing our waterways; we are bringing factories into this country from the United States and are making goods for export to all parts of the world.
Water power development will make us independent of the United States for coal. In developing the deep waterway from Montreal, we would probably not need to go to ocean depth, but we could go to the depth of the Welland canal, and if we have not the whole control of the St. Lawrence

The Budget-Mr. Baldwin
route, we certainly have the whole control of the Welland canal. If this water power is developed, we shall be able to electrify all the railways of Canada, at least so far as Quebec and Ontario are concerned, and have power to supply all our industrial concerns. I know at present of a company that is waiting to come to Canada with fifteen million pounds sterling. They have a factory farther west in Ontario and they are waiting for this power development on the St. Lawrence before opening up a large plant for the manufacture of electrical transmission machinery of every kind from the wheel to the whistle. Let me assure the people of Montreal that I would not advocate any policy that would injure any part of our great country, but I could not imagine that two or three or four hundred million of money could be expended within twenty-five miles of the island of Montreal without practically all of it being spent in and around that city and when the work was completed the population of Montreal would be increased by a million, I believe, and all along the line of development there would be great industrial enterprises.
The benefits of the work would be reflected in every part of the country. My county is 130 miles away from where this great development would take place, but I believe its benefits would be reflected in all the eastern townships as well as in the West. The coal of Alberta would come down that system of waterways and canals to the great provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and the products of the coal and iron mines of Cape Breton would likewise go up that waterway. I go further and say this, although it is somewhat of an accusation against the Opposition: When the powers that were in Newfoundland came to Ottawa to enter Confederation they were turned down through haggling over a paltry sum. The Hon. Mackenzie Bowell was then Prime Minister. Let Canada force her way along and show that she is great-and if you want to know her greatness just go into the United States and see what they think about it; they say, "You do not comprehend yourself. You do not value your country. You do not see your country as we see it"-and then when this work is consummated and we get into closer union with the whole British West Indies, I believe that Newfoundland will enter Confederation. We have to make this a century of great development, and we must not wait for the end of the century before we start.
Now I come to the tariff. Some people seem to be very scared over the budget proposals, but so far as I am concerned,
I am optimistic. Suppose the United States do own sixty per cent of the world's gold, and that they do not want to trade with us. It seems to me when we look around our Empire with nearly five hundred millions of people, and then at our allies in the late war, we need not fear if the United States want to fence themselves in with a high tariff. Let them do it, and we will see who will {be the winner.
1 will guarantee that the United States will not put up any tariff so that they cannot trade with the rest of the world, and that it will come down as soon as they see Canada can stand on her own feet. Very soon we shall be able to go to the Old Country again and negotiate loans to develop our country.
We want to teach our boys and girls that we have something to do in this country besides being Boy Scouts and Girl Guides and Cadets. In olden times the boys and girls were used, and used well, and they made mighty good men and women through helping their fathers and mothers, and learning how to do things. We want them to learn to live within their means, and if they want something, to earn it. Then you get them started right. The great trouble with the country to-day is that we are aping to a large extent that great and rich country, the United States. I do not wish to say anything against the United States, but they know that we are aping the fashions of foolishness, and are forgetting to work and be prudent.
I listened with great interest during the first three weeks of this session to those who call themselves the Progressive party in this House, and I must say that I admire their fair-mindedness, honesty of purpose, and willingness to try and build up this country. As I have said it is geographical differences that separate us, and we must not forget it. It seemed to me to-day that the hori. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Johnston) rather accentuated those differences. I hope he did not mean to. Perhaps I misunderstood him. However, it is ii fact that when that group of manufacturers came to Ottawa in 1877 and asked Hon. Alexander Mackenzie to give them a higher tariff, and he refused, they went down to the Russell Hotel bar, and Sir John Macdonald was there, and in a spirit of joviality said, " Elect me, boys, and I will give you what you want."

speechtext:
That is very
good. Of course, the people in this world are not all philanthropists. Your heart may be right and mine may be right, but it is fair to say that the rich have built up philanthropic institutions. They have built homes for old people, hospitals for crippled children and supported schools and churches. Of course, the money must come from them for the sick. I would like to see unanimity of purpose in our Parliament. People speak of the separation of capital and labour. Capital is just accumulated labour. Everything we use, eat and wear is created by labour, and it is wrong to say anything against labour. The late Minister of Interior told us last year, when he was making his speech, what the different members had said. He said the member for Stanstead would allow anybody to come into the country that was law abiding and willing to work, and he was quite right. I even go further and say that I never saw in my life a dishonest, disreputable, thieving person who would stick continuously to work which he was asked to do. It is the same old doctrine "Satan finds some mischief for idle hands to do." If people look at it properly, there should be no disrespect whatever for the labourer who is willing to work. I would let everybody into this country who is able and willing to work. If the people in British Columbia do not want to associate with the yellow people, that is their business and no concern of mine.
It is conceded by all that this is a great country. We have a railway system that is larger than our population warrants, and it is absolutely necessary that more people shall come to the country. We must therefore be united in improvBiig conditions in
The Budget-Mr. Lewis

Canada so that this country may be advertised abroad as a desirable place for intending immigrants to settle in. We may fight politically, but to the outside world we must present a united front.
